# UltraCompressor II — DOS → Linux port

A Linux port of the **UltraCompressor II** (UC2) DOS sources, plus small
native extractors for UC2 archives.

UC2 is a 1990s MS-DOS archiver by AIP-NL (Ad Infinitum Programs) that combined
LZ-style compression with *shared dictionaries* (masters) to beat ZIP on related
files. Its original source was later released under the LGPL by its author, Nico
de Vries. This tree ports that source to a modern 32/64-bit C++ toolchain and adds
native decoders for UC2 archives, including self-extracting `.EXE` files.

## Repository layout

```
.
├── Makefile          top-level convenience make (builds both sub-projects)
├── LICENSE           GNU LGPL v3
├── original/         original UltraCompressor II DOS sources, as released (AIP-NL)
├── src/              the DOS → Linux port (binary: src/uc2)
│   ├── *.cpp *.h     ported sources (Borland RTL replaced by linux_inc/)
│   ├── linux_inc/    POSIX shims for the Borland run-time (conio, dos, dir, ...)
│   └── super.inc     SUPERMASTER dictionary (needed by uc2_decomp.cpp)
└── unuc2/            native (portable C) UC2 decoders
    ├── libunuc2.c/.h Ultra/UltraComp decoder library
    ├── unuc2.c       CLI: extract standard .UC2 archives
    ├── unuc2sea.c    CLI + API: extract self-extracting .EXE archives
    ├── super.bin     SUPERMASTER data used by the decoder
    ├── VENDORED.md   provenance of the upstream unuc2 code (0.8, unmodified)
    └── super.inc     generated at build time from super.bin
```

## Building

Requirements: `gcc`, `g++`, `hexdump` (util-linux) and `make`.

```bash
make            # build src/uc2 and the unuc2 / unuc2sea tools
make uc2        # only the DOS-port binary (includes the native extractor)
make tools      # only unuc2 + unuc2sea
make test       # build everything, then run an extraction smoke test
make install    # install the binaries under $(PREFIX)/bin (default /usr/local)
make dist       # build source + binary release tarballs in dist/
make clean      # clean all sub-projects
```

## Usage

### `src/uc2` — the ported archiver

```
uc2 a <files...>          add files to an archive
uc2 e <archive> [#dir]    extract an archive (type auto-detected)
uc2 x <archive> [#dir]    same as 'e'
uc2 l <archive>           list an archive
uc2 v <archive>           verbose list
uc2 t <archive>           test/repair an archive
uc2 c <archive>           convert an archive to UC2 format
uc2 split <archive> <KiB> split an archive into <archive>.P01, .P02, ...
uc2 join  <archive>       rebuild an archive from its pieces
```

The extract command auto-detects the input type: a standard `.UC2` archive, or a
self-extracting `.EXE` (its DOS stub is skipped and the embedded archive is decoded
like any other):

```bash
uc2 e archive.uc2                 # extracts into the current directory
uc2 e selfextract.exe '#out'      # extracts a self-extracting .EXE into out/
```

### `unuc2` / `unuc2sea` — standalone extractors

```bash
make -C unuc2
./unuc2/unuc2sea archive.exe output-dir/   # self-extracting .EXE
./unuc2/unuc2     archive.uc2 out/ ./out   # standard .UC2 archive
```

## Multi-volume archives

`uc2 split` / `uc2 join` implement the original **SAS** ("simple archive
splitter") format: pieces are named `archive.P01`, `.P02`, … each with a 14-byte
header, and are **byte-interchangeable** with the original `SAS.EXE` (both
directions verified against the shipped binary).

The piece format was reverse-engineered for interoperability from the original
`SAS.EXE`, which ships in the **UC PRO v2.3** package (`uc2pro.exe`, free for
individual use): <http://www.bttr-software.de/freesoft/arc1.htm> — see also
*Credits & references* below.

```bash
uc2 split archive.uc2 1440     # 1440 KiB pieces (one floppy)
uc2 join  archive.uc2          # rebuild the archive from the pieces
```

## Banners

If an archive carries an ANSI banner (`U$~BAN.TXT`), it is displayed on
extraction

## Status

* Full archiver engine: create / list / test / extract through `src/uc2`,
  verified by round-trip (single file, multi-file and large inputs) and
  cross-checked with the native `unuc2` decoder.
* Long file names are supported on add, list and extract. They are stored in the
  archive with the original `AIP:Win95 LongN` tag, so archives remain
  format-compatible with `unuc2` and the original UC2.
* Native extraction of standard `.UC2` archives and self-extracting `.EXE`
  files, verified byte-for-byte against a reference.
* Multi-volume archives (SAS-compatible `split` / `join`) and native ANSI banners.
* Free software: **no licence or registration required** (GNU LGPL v3).
  management, volume labels, video BIOS). See `src/NOTES.md`.

## Credits & references

This port would not exist without the following people and projects.

* **Original UltraCompressor II** © 1992–1996 **AIP-NL (Ad Infinitum Programs)**,
  by **Nico de Vries** together with **Danny Bezemer** and **Jan-Pieter Cornet**
  and many other contributors. The author re-released the source under the
  **GNU LGPL** (December 2015): <https://www.nicodevries.com/professional/>
* The full list of everyone who contributed to UC2 (ideas, work, support,
  testing, …) is in the `CREDITS` section of [`src/U_MANUAL.TXT`](src/U_MANUAL.TXT).
* **Native `unuc2` decoders** © **Jan Bobrowski** 2020–2022 (LGPL v3):
  <https://torinak.com/~jb/unuc2/> · <https://github.com/jan-bobrowski/unuc2>
  — vendored unmodified (v0.8), see [`unuc2/VENDORED.md`](unuc2/VENDORED.md).
* **`mem.h`** additionally carries grants to **Jean-loup Gailly** and
  **Robert Jung** (the gzip authors), with parts © 1993 **Jan-Pieter Cornet**.
* **SAS** ("simple archive splitter") ships with **UC PRO v2.3** (`uc2pro.exe`,
  free for individual use) and was the reference for the byte-compatible
  `split` / `join`. Its own source is not part of the LGPL release:
  <http://www.bttr-software.de/freesoft/arc1.htm>
* **Linux port** by **Manuel FLURY** (2026).

**License:** GNU Lesser General Public License v3 — see [`LICENSE`](LICENSE)

# Ultima V Web

*Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny* (the 1988 MS-DOS version) in your web browser.

**Play it here: https://linupa.github.io/ultimaVWeb/**

This is a JavaScript port of [ultimaVSDL](https://github.com/linupa/ultimaVSDL), a C++ port made
from the decompiled original. It plays the whole game: the title sequence and character
creation, Britannia and its towns, conversations and shops, combat and magic, the dungeons and
shrines, and the endings. It looks and sounds like the original on an EGA card with the PC
speaker.

## You need your own copy of the game

**This site contains none of the game's data** - no pictures, maps, text or music. It reads them
from your own copy of Ultima V, which must be the **IBM PC (MS-DOS) version**. Versions for other
machines (Apple II, Commodore 64, Atari ST, Amiga, ...) use different file formats and won't work.

You can recognise the right files by `ULTIMA.EXE`, `DATA.OVL` and the other `.OVL` files,
`TILES.16`, `BRIT.DAT` and `INIT.GAM`. If your copy came on several floppy disks, put the contents
of all of them in one folder. Upper or lower case file names are both fine. A ZIP file of the
game works too: the page takes the files from the folder in it that holds `DATA.OVL`.

Your files stay in your browser. Nothing is uploaded anywhere.

## Playing

1. Open the page and click **Choose the Ultima V folder**, then pick the folder with the game's
   files - or click **Or a ZIP of it** and pick a ZIP file of the game, which is unpacked in your
   browser. The browser remembers the files, so this is needed only once.
2. The game starts as the original does: the Origin logo, Lord British's signature, the title and
   the menu. Choose **Create New Character** to start a new game, or **Journey Onward** to carry
   on with the saved game in your folder. The original's **Transfer from Ultima IV** is now
   **Load/Save/Transfer Game**, for the saved games (below).

You need a keyboard; the game is played with keys, as on DOS. Before the game the mouse works
too: a click skips the title sequence and the demo, turns the introduction's pages and closes the
acknowledgements, and a click on a menu item chooses it. In character creation, Male or Female
and the gypsy's answers can be clicked: the choice under the pointer is shown in inverted colours,
like the menu's cursor, which follows the mouse. On a touch screen every choice is outlined. As with
buttons, a click or tap counts when it is released: while pressed, the item under the pointer
lights up (in the menu, the menu's own cursor moves to it) and follows a drag, and releasing
elsewhere chooses nothing.

In Britannia and in towns, pressing the map moves the party one step that way, as an arrow key
does - at once, without waiting for the release. A press off to a diagonal goes the nearest of the
four ways. Held for half a second or more, the party keeps walking until you let go, towards
wherever the pointer or finger is, so a drag steers it - except from the squares right next to the
party, which give one step.

The four squares right next to the party (not diagonally) also have the commands that ask for a
direction. A quick click or tap on one steps there; held for half a second, it opens a ring of the
commands around the square: Talk, Look, Attack, Get, Open, Search, Push, Jimmy
and Klimb. Slide onto one
and let go, or let go and then click one, to do it towards the square. A click outside the ring or
any key closes it.

Held for half a second on the party itself, the press opens two rings of the other commands: Enter,
Board, X-it, Cast, Use, Ready and Ztats inside; Hole up, Ignite torch, Mix, New order, View,
Yell, Pass and Save (Quit & save) outside. Whenever the game asks for a direction - for a command
typed on the keyboard, say - a click or tap on a square next to the party answers it. When the game asks anything else (which item, yes
or no...), a click or tap on the map cancels it, as Escape does (a direction question gets Pass).

On a screen taller than wide (a phone held upright), the game's windows are rearranged to fit it:
the map across the top, the status window below it on the left and the text window on the right.
The title, the menu and character creation keep the original screen. Turn the phone sideways for
the original layout in the game too.

On a phone or tablet, the screen keyboard opens when the game asks you to type (your name, a
conversation, an amount); if it doesn't, tap the screen - in the game, the text window (bottom
right). A tap on the text window opens it any time, for typing commands too; a tap on the map or
the status window hides it. Walking and the commands work by touching the map (above).

- **Arrow keys** move; the letters **A**-**Z** are the commands (Attack, Board, Cast, Enter, Fire,
  Get, Hole up, Ignite torch, Jimmy, Klimb, Look, Mix, New order, Open, Push, Quit & save, Ready,
  Search, Talk, Use, View, X-it, Yell, Ztats). **1**-**6** pick the active player, **0** clears it.
- **Ctrl+S** turns the sound on or off. Sound starts after your first key press (browsers don't
  let a page play sound before that).
- **Ctrl+R**, **Ctrl+W**, **Ctrl+T**, **Ctrl+N**, **Ctrl+L** and **Ctrl+Q** are left to the browser.
- In combat, aim with the arrow keys; **Home**, **End**, **Page Up** and **Page Down** aim
  diagonally.

### Saving

**Q** saves the game, as in the original. The save is kept in your browser, and it is what
**Journey Onward** loads next time. In the menu, **Load/Save/Transfer Game** (or the key **T** or
**L**) opens a second menu:

- **Download Saved Game** gives you `SAVED.GAM` and `SAVED.OOL`. They work in the original game
  too.
- **Load a Saved Game** asks for a `SAVED.GAM` (and `SAVED.OOL`) from your computer - from the
  original game, for example, or one downloaded earlier, even if it was renamed `SAVED (1).GAM`.
  **Journey Onward** then plays it.
- **Transfer from Ultima IV** - below.
- **Return** (or Escape) goes back to the menu.

Clearing the site's data in your browser also deletes your saves, so download the ones you want
to keep.

### Transfer from Ultima IV

To bring your hero over from Ultima IV, pick **Transfer from Ultima IV** in the
**Load/Save/Transfer Game** menu and choose Ultima IV's `PARTY.SAV`.

### Shortcuts

Add these to the address:

- `?m` - start at the menu, skipping the title sequence.
- `?j` - go straight into the saved game (Journey Onward).

## What isn't there yet

- Only the EGA look. The C++ port can also look like the CGA and Hercules versions; this one
  can't.
- Some questions can't be answered by touch yet (choosing a party member, yes or no): on a phone,
  open the screen keyboard from the text window.

## Development

You need [Node.js](https://nodejs.org/) 22.

```sh
npm install
npm run dev     # a local server with hot reload
npm test        # the tests (Vitest)
npm run build   # the static site, in dist/
```

`npm run dev` also serves your copy of the game from `../ultima5` (or the folder in the
`U5_GAME` environment variable), so the page doesn't have to ask for it. The tests that need the
game's files read them from the same place and are skipped when it isn't there.

**Never commit the game's files.** `.gitignore` keeps them out of the repository.

### How the code is organised

The port follows the C++ port's structure module by module, and through it the original's: the
comments cite the original's routines by address (e.g. `/** 5a28 */`). Everything that waits for
time or a key is `async`.

| Where | What |
|---|---|
| `src/main.js`, `src/store.js`, `src/gamefiles.js`, `src/zip.js` | the page: choosing the game folder or ZIP, saves in IndexedDB |
| `src/platform/` | the browser: canvas, keyboard, timers, Web Audio |
| `src/data/` | reading `DATA.OVL`, the strings, LZW-compressed pictures |
| `src/video/`, `src/gfx.js`, `src/text.js`, `src/tiles.js`, `src/picture.js` | EGA graphics and text |
| `src/game.js`, `src/outdoor.js`, `src/town.js`, `src/dungeon.js` | the game loops |
| `src/combat.js`, `src/magic.js`, `src/stats.js`, `src/talk.js`, `src/shops.js`, ... | the rest of the game |
| `src/intro.js`, `src/endings.js` | the title, menu and character creation; death and the endings |
| `test/` | the tests |
| `tools/reference/` | checks against the C++ port (see its README) |

`tools/gen-string-ids.py` makes `src/data/string-ids.js` (names and offsets only, no text) from
the C++ port's `strings.h`.

### Checking against the C++ port

With [ultimaVSDL](https://github.com/linupa/ultimaVSDL) built in `../ultima5_sdl` and the game in
`../ultima5`, the scripts in `tools/reference/` play the same key sequences in both ports, with the
same random seeds, and compare the screen, the text and the saved game (with the original's menu:
Transfer from Ultima IV in place of Load/Save/Transfer Game). 45 scenarios cover the title and
menu, towns, conversations and shops, fights, magic, dungeons, shrines, death and the ending:

```sh
python3 tools/reference/variants.py ../ultima5   # saved games the scenarios start from
tools/reference/check-all.sh
```

## Publishing on GitHub Pages

`.github/workflows/deploy.yml` tests and builds the site and publishes it on every push to `main`.
To turn it on, set **Settings > Pages > Source** to **GitHub Actions** in the repository. The site
works under any repository name (the build uses relative paths); its address is
`https://<user>.github.io/<repository>/`.

## License

The code is under the [MIT License](LICENSE). The license covers this project's code only, not
Ultima V itself.

## Credits

*Ultima V: Warriors of Destiny* is © 1988 Origin Systems; Ultima is a trademark of Electronic Arts.
This project is not affiliated with or endorsed by them, and it includes none of the game's
content: it needs your own copy of the game to run.

# OpenPizza 0.1

A native C/SDL2 reconstruction of Pizza Tycoon for Windows x64 and macOS.

The game loads graphics, fonts, sound, music and initial tables directly from
**your own Pizza Tycoon English DOS V2.0 installation**. Original game assets
and executables are not distributed. No startup bundle or emulator is required.

Windows: extract the release ZIP, copy the original game directory to `PIZZA`
beside `PizzaTycoon.exe`, and run the launcher. `PT_GAME_DATA_DIR` may point to
another game directory. If the files are missing or incompatible, the game offers
an optional download from the [Internet Archive](https://archive.org/details/msdos_Pizza_Tycoon_1994).
Choose **Download** to install the verified files in your user data folder, or
**Cancel** to leave without downloading. No game data is bundled with OpenPizza.
Saves and logs are stored under `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Pizza Tycoon`.

The public 0.1 checks cover startup, New Game through the city map, and native
save/load. Complete campaign playthroughs and broader regression comparisons
have not yet been repeated on this public build.
Windows builds are smoke-tested with Wine; testing on Windows hardware is pending.

On macOS install SDL2 and run:

```sh
make native
./build/pizza-native --data /path/to/PIZZA
```

All 495 fixed resource files are checked by SHA-256 before play.
The downloader also checks the exact ZIP and executable fingerprints, installs
only the required resources, and never runs the downloaded DOS executable.
Downloaded data is reused on later launches. Existing files are never overwritten.
On Windows it is stored below `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Pizza Tycoon\game-data`; on macOS,
below `~/Library/Application Support/Pizza Tycoon/game-data`.
If an existing managed folder is damaged, a new numbered folder is used.
You can still supply your own installation without downloading anything.

For an explicit download or offline installation of the same verified archive:

```sh
./build/pizza-native --download-data /new/path/PIZZA
./build/pizza-native --install-data-archive Pizza_Tycoon_1994.zip /new/path/PIZZA
```

All downloaded input is validated before the installation becomes available. The unmodified
English V2.0 `PT.EXE` (or `PT_Original.EXE`) must be 470411 bytes with SHA-256
`9cce82355b466fc0e47c51ae1de4ba850a666b5f12c3831ee19ba5c4c4ef6add`.
The executable is read as data to extract initial tables; it is never executed.
Other languages and game revisions are not supported by this release.

`tools/resources.py` converts graphics to labeled PNG sprite sheets, sound to
WAV, and music to editable event/instrument tables. It reconstructs the selected
original media files exactly; see `tools/resource_formats/README.md`.

The source is organized into subsystem files. Include `pizza.h` for the main
application API or the subsystem header listed in `SOURCE_LAYOUT.md`.

Program source: GPL v3 only, copyright 2026 Drevton. The OPL chip model retains
its LGPL license and attribution. The bundled puff inflater retains its zlib license. Original game data retains its owners' rights.

# Fountain of Dreams Reversing

Fountain of Dreams reverse engineering resources. Fountain of Dreams was a 16
bit DOS game released in 1990 by Electronic Arts.

Additional information: [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fountain_of_Dreams)

* [Internal documentation](https://devinsmith.github.io/fod)

The game executables (fod.exe) and (keh.exe) are packed using Microsoft
EXEPACK and can be unpacked with the [unEXEPACK](https://github.com/w4kfu/unEXEPACK) project.

# Progress

This repo can display the title screen (TPICT), handle character creation, and
allows movement on the map.

# Building

Install dependencies first:

VoidLinux

```
sudo xbps-install -S SDL2-devel
```

Debian

```
sudo apt install libsdl2-dev
```

Then use CMake to build:

```
mkdir build
cd build
cmake ..
make
```

The `fod` binary will be in build/src/fe/fod

Other flags can be passed to CMake:

* `ENABLE_TESTS=ON/OFF` toggles building unit tests (Requires Check). OFF by default.
* `ENABLE_TOOLS=ON/OFF` toggles building some extra tools for extracting resources. OFF by default.


# Code Quality

The code in this repo might not follow best practices at the moment. The
intention is for the C code to match the disassembly closely. That means if the
original disassembly allocated memory into global variables, the C code does
this as well. Once most of the code is reverse engineered, we may start
cleaning this up to follow best practices.

Please do not submit PRs to "clean up the code" until this notice is removed.

chesterbr-a-busca-de-epaminondas-jr-read.text: # A Busca de Epaminondas Jr. Em 1992 publiquei este adventure de texto para MS-DOS, feito em Turbo Basic 1.0: você é Epaminondas e precisa achar o disquete do chefe para não perder o emprego. Na época distribuí só o executável, e o código-fonte se perdeu. Influenciado pelo burburinho recente em torno do [Reverse Engineer Anything](https://github.com/morluto/rea), resolvi fazer o disassembly e reconstruir o fonte, assistido por IA. O resultado: - **[LEGIVEL.BAS](basic/gerado/LEGIVEL.BAS)** **(comece por aqui)**: o fonte do jogo, comentado e formatado. - **[CA1.BAS](basic/gerado/CA1.BAS)**: o fonte mais próximo do original, que recompila para o executável idêntico byte a byte. - **[epa.py](python/epa.py)**: uma implementação de referência em Python, de linha de comando. O repositório também tem o [jogo original](original/), o [disassembly](analise/) e a [documentação do processo](docs/engenharia-reversa.md). E dá para jogar no navegador: - [o original](https://chester.me/a-busca-de-epaminondas-jr/original.html) (via [js-dos](https://js-dos.com/), um DOSBox em WebAssembly) - [a versão Python](https://chester.me/a-busca-de-epaminondas-jr/python.html) (via [Pyodide](https://pyodide.org/) e [xterm.js](https://xtermjs.org/)) | :-:|:-: Original | Versão Python (terminal) > **In English:** a 1992 Brazilian Portuguese text adventure written in Turbo Basic 1.0, whose source was lost (I only distributed the executable). With AI help I disassembled it and rebuilt the source: a readable, commented version, one that recompiles to a byte-identical executable, and a Python reimplementation checked against the original in DOSBox-X, plus the original files, notes and memory dumps. Play [the original](https://chester.me/a-busca-de-epaminondas-jr/original.html) or [the Python version](https://chester.me/a-busca-de-epaminondas-jr/python.html) in the browser. Portuguese only. ## Jogar localmente A versão Python não tem dependências, só o Python 3.9 ou mais novo: ``` python3 python/epa.py ``` Ela aceita um arquivo com os comandos, como a [solução completa](python/caminhos/00_caminho_feliz.txt) (SPOILERS): ``` python3 python/epa.py python/caminhos/00_caminho_feliz.txt ``` Para o original, use o DOSBox (ou DOSBox-X): ``` dosbox -c "mount c original" -c "c:" -c "aventura.bat" ``` Troque `aventura.bat` por `ca1.exe` para pular a abertura. Os jogos gravados (`*.CA1`) ficam salvos. ## Engenharia reversa Feita com o Claude Code e estas ferramentas: - Um decodificador em Python (com [capstone](https://www.capstone-engine.org/)) para desmontar o `CA1.EXE`, que tem chamadas ao runtime com operandos embutidos (`basic/gerar.py`). - O DOSBox-X e seu depurador (`BPINT`, `MEMDUMPBIN`), para extrair a memória do jogo rodando e comparar com a reimplementação. - O Turbo Basic 1.0 ([WinWorld](https://winworldpc.com/product/turbo-basic/1x)), para compilar programas de teste e ver o que o compilador gera (`basic/rosetta/`). Comece por `docs/engenharia-reversa.md`. ## O que tem aqui | Pasta | Conteúdo | |---|---| | [`original/`](original/) | Os arquivos de 1992, com `SHA256SUMS`, o [epa15.zip](https://chester.me/download/epa15.zip) de onde saíram e cópias em UTF-8 dos textos | | [`analise/`](analise/) | Dumps de memória, listagem do código, tabelas e pseudocódigo de salas e verbos | | [`basic/`](basic/) | Os fontes Turbo Basic, o gerador a partir do executável e a "Pedra de Roseta" do compilador (`rosetta/`) | | [`python/`](python/) | A reimplementação, os 45 roteiros de teste e as saídas esperadas | | [`web/`](web/) | As páginas para jogar no navegador e o `montar.py`, que monta o site do GitHub Pages | | [`docs/`](docs/engenharia-reversa.md) | Como o jogo funciona por dentro e os testes feitos no original | | [`ferramentas/dosbox/`](ferramentas/dosbox/) | Scripts (macOS) que pilotam o original no DOSBox-X para comparar com a reimplementação | ## Testes Um comando roda tudo (os 45 roteiros contra as saídas esperadas, mais a conferência dos textos): ``` python3 python/testar.py ``` As saídas esperadas foram conferidas contra o original rodando no DOSBox-X (ver `python/caminhos/LEIA.md`). Se uma mudança de comportamento for de propósito, `python3 python/testar.py --atualizar` regrava as saídas e o diff do git mostra o que mudou. ## Fidelidade e diferenças O `CA1.BAS` e o `LEGIVEL.BAS` reproduzem o executável como ele é, bugs inclusive. O `epa.py` também segue o original, com poucas diferenças propositais, listadas em `docs/engenharia-reversa.md` e `python/erratas.md`: os textos foram modernizados (acentos, aspas, pontuação; o original usava CP437, sem `ã` e `õ`), e dois erros óbvios foram corrigidos (a frase "MESMO ???", engolida por um bug, e `LER PLACA` no elevador). O `MENU` do jogo não foi reimplementado. ## Licença Código, ferramentas e documentos deste repositório: [MIT](LICENSE). O jogo original é de domínio público, por declaração minha em `original/AVENTURA.BAT` ("Este é um programa de domínio público. A cópia é livre e autorizada.").

denissergeevitch-pole-chudes-2-readme-md.text: # Поле Чудес 2 — DOS-first TypeScript port A faithful browser port of **Pole Chudes 2** (Вадим «Дима» Башуров, 1993) — the classic Russian DOS game show — written in TypeScript. The original source code is lost; this port reimplements the complete game from its original binary assets and a public-domain disassembly-based reconstruction, scene for scene: splash intro, player presentation with name entry, eight tournament stages (1/64 ФИНАЛА → СУПЕРФИНАЛ), the 16-sector wheel, hand-cursor letter picking, the assistant flipping letters on the board, the шкатулки minigame, prize bargaining with Якубович, ad breaks, the endgame ceremony, and the top-8 table. ![Gameplay](docs/screenshot.png) ## Run it ```bash cd web npm install npm run dev # open the printed URL ``` URL parameters: `?seed=42` reproduces a whole game deterministically, `?fast=10` scales every delay (useful for testing). Controls (as in DOS): **Space / click** — confirm and skip pauses, **←/→** — move the hand, **Enter** — accept name/word entry, **letters** — type text, **Ctrl+S** — sound on/off (off by default, as in DOS), **Tab** — boss-key mute, **Alt+Enter** — fullscreen, **Esc** — new game. The **Admin Panel** tab hosts a session-scoped question editor with import/export of binary-correct `POLE.OVL` files. ## Verify ```bash cd web npm run test # 93 unit + integration tests, incl. seeded headless full games npm run build npm run smoke # Playwright: splash → name entry → spin → letter → solve npm run verify # all of the above ``` ## How it works - `web/src/assets/` — codecs for the original data formats: `POLE2.LIB` (row-RLE sprites), `POLE.FNT` (8px bitmap fonts ×3 heights), `POLE.OVL` (encoded question dictionary), `POLE.PIC` (top-8 table). The shipped assets are editable transcodes of those files — graphics as lossless WebP images (one per sprite, plus font glyph atlases, openable in any image editor) with slim JSON manifests, question text and scores as JSON — each proven to rebuild its original byte-for-byte (sha256-pinned in tests). - `web/src/engine/` — the "DOS machine": a linear 640×750 indexed framebuffer with the original's back-buffer scratch regions, sprite/glyph/fill/copy primitives, a 50 fps presenter, Win32-style auto-reset key events, an 8 kHz PWM square-wave audio synth, an abortable clock, and the Borland LCG for seed-exact randomness. - `web/src/game/script.ts` — a direct port of the original main loop, with `dpr:NNN` comments citing the reference source line by line. - `web/src/spec/` — machine-readable facts (formats, palette, geometry, sector dispatch) plus a parity-case ledger, pinned by tests. Design and fidelity policy: [`docs/architecture.md`](docs/architecture.md). Accepted deviations from the DOS original: [`DIFF_FROM_ORIGINAL.md`](DIFF_FROM_ORIGINAL.md). Research notes and evidence trail: [`reverse-engineering/`](reverse-engineering/). ## Zero binaries: the whole game is editable source The original game was five opaque binary files (178,777 bytes). This repo ships **none of them** — every byte is converted to a source format a human can open and edit, and every conversion is proven lossless: - **POLE2.EXE** (56,528 B of 16-bit code) → TypeScript. The executable is not shipped or executed; its behavior lives in `web/src/engine/` and `web/src/game/script.ts`, cross-referenced line-by-line against the public-domain reconstruction. - **POLE2.LIB** (61 RLE-compressed sprites) → 61 lossless WebP images in [`web/public/assets/sprites/`](web/public/assets/sprites/) — the spinning wheel on the right is four of them — plus a slim JSON manifest for the bytes an image can't carry (sprite order and the original packer's stale-buffer padding, preserved verbatim). - **POLE.FNT** (3 bitmap fonts) → three WebP glyph atlases in [`web/public/assets/fonts/`](web/public/assets/fonts/) (16×16 CP866 glyphs each, white = bit set). - **POLE.OVL** (686 encoded questions) and **POLE.PIC** (top-8 table) → plain JSON with the question text readable in any editor. The trick that keeps this honest: the build can run the conversion in reverse. `web/src/assets/transcoded.test.ts` re-encodes the WebP pixels through the inferred row-RLE packer and rebuilds each original file **byte-for-byte** (sha256-pinned; the originals themselves stay in a gitignored `_local/` directory as test fixtures). Edit a sprite and the game happily runs your fork — but the fidelity tests will tell you it's no longer the 1993 original. ## Attribution and asset note - Behavioral reference: the public-domain (Unlicense) Delphi reconstruction [fersatgit/Pole2](https://github.com/fersatgit/Pole2), built by disassembling the original `POLE2.exe`. A UTF-8 decoded copy lives in [`reference/delphi/`](reference/delphi/) with matching line numbers. - `web/public/assets/` contains the original 1993 game data (`POLE2.LIB`, `POLE.FNT`, `POLE.OVL`, `POLE.PIC`) © Вадим Башуров, transcoded to editable sources (lossless WebP images for the graphics, JSON for the rest) that rebuild the original binaries byte-for-byte — the transcode changes the format, not the provenance. The data is included for preservation and is required to run the game; no original executable code is shipped or executed. If you are a rights holder and want it removed, open an issue. - The TypeScript code in this repository is original work, released under the MIT license ([`LICENSE`](LICENSE)); the license does not extend to the transcoded 1993 game data.

# Skybuck's Civilization 1 for Turbo Pascal / Borland Pascal 7.01

> **A period-accurate port of the original 1991 *Sid Meier's Civilization* from C to Turbo Pascal 7.01 (and Borland Pascal 7.01).**

This repository contains a **work-in-progress** conversion of the reverse-engineered C source code of Civilization 1 (the `sjmelia/civd` project) into Turbo Pascal / Borland Pascal 7.01, targeting MS-DOS 6.22. The ultimate goal is to produce a Pascal-native, almost byte-for-byte equivalent of the original game that can be compiled, debugged, and extended with the legendary Borland toolchain.

---

## Table of Contents

1. [Project Goal](#1-project-goal)
2. [Repository Structure](#2-repository-structure)
3. [Restoring the Game Data](#3-restoring-the-game-data)
4. [Build vs. Run: two separate concerns](#4-build-vs-run-two-separate-concerns)
5. [Required Tools & Where to Get Them](#5-required-tools--where-to-get-them)
6. [Setting Up DOSBox-X](#6-setting-up-dosbox-x)
7. [How the Batch Files Work](#7-how-the-batch-files-work)
8. [Testing Architecture](#8-testing-architecture)
9. [Build & Debug Architecture (Log Files)](#9-build--debug-architecture-log-files)
10. [Current State of the Pascal Code](#10-current-state-of-the-pascal-code)
11. [Using This Project with an AI Agent](#11-using-this-project-with-an-ai-agent)
12. [Generated Folders & Files](#12-generated-folders--files)
13. [MASM in This Project](#13-masm-in-this-project)
14. [Target Environment](#14-target-environment)
15. [Notes and Ideas](#15-notes-and-ideas)
16. [References](#16-references)

---

## 1. Project Goal

The original *Civilization* was written in C and compiled with Microsoft C. The `sjmelia/civd` project successfully reverse-engineered the source into buildable C code. This project takes that C code and **translates it, line-by-line, into Turbo Pascal 7.01 / Borland Pascal 7.01** - a language and IDE that many retro developers consider far more pleasant than the Microsoft C toolchain of the era.

The motivation is threefold:

1. **Debugging & maintainability** - Turbo Pascal 7.01 ships with Turbo Debugger 3.2 (`TDX.EXE`), which can step into assembly and overlay code, making it easier to track down the infamous "phantom unit" bugs of Civilization 1.
2. **Overlay management** - Turbo Pascal's built-in overlay system (`$O+`) simplifies the segment/overlay gymnastics that the original C code had to handle manually.
3. **Historical curiosity** - Could Sid Meier have used Turbo Pascal instead of C? This project tries to answer that question in practice.

The long-term vision includes 512-unit support, bug fixes for AI unit starvation, and eventually a fully Pascal-native codebase (the assembly helpers are still being converted).

---

## 2. Repository Structure

```
Civ1Pas/
├── asm/                     # MASM 5.10 assembly sources (resident, graphics, sound, etc.)
├── data/                    # Original game data files (PIC, PAL, TXT, FONTS.CV)
├── src/                     # Turbo Pascal source units and the main program
├── tests/                   # Auto-generated compile-test stubs (created by mktests.pas)
│   ├── src/                 # t_<unit>.pas stubs
│   └── tpuexe/              # Compiled .TPU / .EXE test artifacts
├── obj/                     # Assembled .OBJ files (release)
├── dbg_obj/                 # Assembled .OBJ files (debug)
├── build/                   # Release output (CIV.EXE, CIV.OVR, drivers, data)
├── dbg_bld/                 # Debug output
├── units/                   # Compiled .TPU files from the build
├── asm.bat                  # Assembles all ASM sources
├── build.bat                # Full release build
├── debug.bat                # Full debug build
├── linkdrv.bat              # Links the ASM drivers (MGRAPHIC.EXE, MISC.EXE, NSOUND.CVL)
├── collect.bat              # Concatenates all sources into conversion.txt
├── mkgen.bat                # Compiles and optionally runs mktests.pas
├── mktests.pas              # Generates test stubs
├── tst.bat                  # Compiles a single unit / stub
├── tests.bat                # Runs the whole compile-test suite
└── conversion.txt           # Single-file concatenation of the whole project (build artifact)
```

> **Note:** The folder layout mirrors the paths used in the batch files (e.g. `L:\Source\Games\Civ1\github repo based on v010\`). Adjust the drive letters in the batch files to match your own environment.

The `data/` folder is **not tracked** - see [3. Restoring the Game Data](#3-restoring-the-game-data) for the files to supply.

---

## 3. Restoring the Game Data

The `data/` folder is **not tracked** (see `.gitignore`). It must be populated from a legitimate **Civilization 1** installation before the game will *run* (though the *build* does not need it - see [4. Build vs. Run](#4-build-vs-run-two-separate-concerns)).

Copy the following files from the original game into `data/`:

| Files | Purpose |
| :--- | :--- |
| `FONTS.CV` | Font glyphs - **required**, the game will not start without it. |
| `*.PIC` | Pictures and sprites (leaders, cities, terrain, wonders, ...). |
| `*.PAL` | Palettes; every `.PIC` that needs a non-default palette has a matching `.PAL`. |
| `*.TXT` | Help text, news, blurb, king dialogue. |

`build.bat` and `debug.bat` copy these four groups into `build\` on every build. An empty `data/` still produces a `CIV.EXE`, but it will fail at the first `file_exists('fonts.cv', ...)` check in `ovintro.pas` and never reach the main menu.

> If you don't have an original install, the same file set is preserved in [`sjmelia/civd`](https://github.com/sjmelia/civd).

---

## 4. Build vs. Run: two separate concerns

The `data/` files are **runtime inputs only**. The build itself is completely data-independent:

- **`asm.bat`** (MASM) never opens a `.PIC`/`.PAL`/`.TXT`/`FONTS.CV` file. All `INCLUDE`s are `.INC` files in `asm/`; there is no `INCBIN`, no `$L` data embedding.
- **`linkdrv.bat`** (LINK) only links `.OBJ` files together into `.EXE`/`.CVL`.
- **`tpc.exe src\*.pas`** (TPC) never `{$I}`s a data file - the only `{$I` directives in the source are `{$I-}`/`{$I+}` (I/O checking toggles).
- **The `build.bat` copy step** is guarded by `if exist data\...`, so a missing `data/` is silently skipped and the build still reports `BUILD SUCCESSFUL`.

The Pascal code references `data/` files **only by name at runtime** - e.g. `load_screen(1, 'birth0.pic')`, `load_palette('sp256.pal', ...)`, `news_name('king.txt', ...)`, `Assign(f, 'credits.txt')`, `run_program(load_program(@graphics_driver, 'fonts.cv'))`. Nothing is inlined into the compiled binary.

The result: **`build\civ.exe` links fine with an empty `data\`, but refuses to start.** This mirrors the original 1991 game, which also checked for its data disk at startup rather than embedding the files. The infinite "Please insert Disk 1" loop in `ovintro.pas` is the exact same behaviour.

---

## 5. Required Tools & Where to Get Them

| Tool | Version | Purpose | Download |
|------|---------|---------|----------|
| **Turbo Pascal** | 7.01 | Lightweight IDE / compiler | [WinWorld: Borland Turbo Pascal 7.x](https://winworldpc.com/product/turbo-pascal/7x) |
| **Borland Pascal with Objects** | 7.01 | Heavier IDE with Turbo Debugger 3.2 (`TDX.EXE`) | [WinWorld: Borland Pascal](https://winworldpc.com/product/borland-pascal) |
| **Microsoft Macro Assembler (MASM)** | **5.10** | Assembles the `.ASM` files | [WinWorld: MASM 5.1](https://winworldpc.com/product/macro-assembler/5x) |
| **DOSBox-X** | Latest | DOS emulator (superior to vanilla DOSBox for development) | [DOSBox-X Releases](https://github.com/joncampbell123/dosbox-x/releases) |
| **Turbo Pascal 7 Language Guide** | - | Language reference | [turbopascal.org PDF](https://turbopascal.org/wp-content/uploads/Turbo_Pascal_Version_7.0_Language_Guide_1992.pdf) |
| **MASM 5.0 Programmer's Guide** | - | Assembly reference | [bitsavers PDF](https://dn721802.ca.archive.org/0/items/bitsavers_microsoftm1987410610014500R000787MASM5.0Programmer_54026053/410610014-500-R00-0787_MASM_5.0_Programmers_Guide_198707.pdf) |

> **Why MASM 5.10?** MASM 6.xx and later introduce byte-sequence differences that break the byte-for-byte equivalence with the original game. **MASM 5.10 is mandatory.**

---

## 6. Setting Up DOSBox-X

DOSBox-X is the recommended emulator because it handles floppy-disk image mounting and disk-swapping far more gracefully than vanilla DOSBox.

### 6.1 Install DOSBox-X

Download the latest release for your platform from the [official GitHub releases page](https://github.com/joncampbell123/dosbox-x/releases).

### 6.2 Install Turbo Pascal / Borland Pascal from floppy images

Both Turbo Pascal 7.01 and Borland Pascal 7.01 ship as floppy-disk images (`disk01.img`, `disk02.img`, ...). Inside DOSBox-X:

```dos
IMGMOUNT A disk01.img disk02.img disk03.img ...
```

Then run the installer from the `A:` drive. When the installer prompts for the next disk, **use DOSBox-X's "Swap Disk" feature** - manually ejecting and re-inserting images often fails.

> **Tip:** If you are installing Borland Pascal with Objects 7.01, the installation is identical; the only difference is the presence of `TDX.EXE` (Turbo Debugger 3.2) and additional protected-mode tools.

### 6.3 Install MASM 5.10

Extract the MASM 5.10 archive into a directory (e.g. `L:\Tools\MASM\v5.10`). No installer is required - just ensure `MASM.EXE` and `LINK.EXE` are in your `PATH` or referenced explicitly by the batch files.

### 6.4 Recommended IDE: `TPX.EXE` vs `TDX.EXE`

- **`TPX.EXE`** - Turbo Pascal IDE in protected mode. Lightweight, handles more memory than the real-mode IDE.
- **`TDX.EXE`** - Turbo Debugger 3.2. The most advanced option: you can step **into assembly** and **into overlay code**. It feels remarkably like modern Delphi.

For pure development, `TPX.EXE` is sufficient. For deep debugging of the ASM helpers or overlay transitions, use `TDX.EXE`.

---

## 7. How the Batch Files Work

All batch files are designed to be run from the **project root** inside DOSBox-X. They assume a directory layout similar to the original author's:

```
L:\Source\Games\Civ1\github repo based on v010\
L:\Tools\TURBOPAS\BIN\
L:\Tools\MASM\v5.10\BIN\
```

> **Important:** You must edit the `set` statements at the top of each batch file to point to **your** tool directories.

### 7.1 `asm.bat`

Assembles every `.ASM` file in `asm/` using MASM 5.10.

- `asm.bat rel` -> outputs `.OBJ` files into `obj/`
- `asm.bat dbg` -> outputs `.OBJ` files into `dbg_obj/` with debug symbols (`/Zd`)

It **fails fast**: if any assembly fails, it jumps to `:fail` and exits with an error level.

### 7.2 `linkdrv.bat`

Links the assembled ASM objects into the driver executables:

| Output | Source |
|--------|--------|
| `MGRAPHIC.EXE` | `mgraphic.obj` |
| `MISC.EXE` | `misc.obj` |
| `NSOUND.CVL` | `asound.obj` |

- `linkdrv.bat rel` -> writes to `build/`
- `linkdrv.bat dbg` -> writes to `dbg_bld/`

### 7.3 `build.bat`

The **full release build**. It:

1. Deletes old output files (`.EXE`, `.OVR`, `.CVL`, `.TPU`, `.OBJ`, etc.).
2. Calls `asm.bat rel` (assembly).
3. Calls `linkdrv.bat rel` (driver linking).
4. Compiles **every Pascal unit** in dependency order using `TPC.EXE`.
5. Renames `civprog.exe` -> `civ.exe` and `civprog.ovr` -> `civ.ovr`.
6. Copies `data/` files into `build/`. (See [3. Restoring the Game Data](#3-restoring-the-game-data) - a fresh clone needs `data/` populated first, or step 6 will copy nothing.)
7. Writes a complete log to `bld.log`.

### 7.4 `debug.bat`

Identical to `build.bat` but:

- Uses `asm.bat dbg` and `linkdrv.bat dbg`.
- Adds `/V /DDEBUG /$L+ /$R+ /$S+ /$I+` to the compiler flags (debug info, range checking, stack checking, I/O checking).
- Outputs to `dbg_bld/` and logs to `dbg.log`.

### 7.5 `tests.bat` / `tst.bat` / `mktests.pas`

These implement the **compile-test suite** (see the next section).

### 7.6 `collect.bat`

A convenience script that concatenates **all** `.bat`, `.pas`, `.asm`, `.inc`, and `conversion.txt` files into a single `conversion.txt`. This is useful for feeding the entire project to an AI agent or for archival.

(concatall.exe tool not supplied)

---

## 8. Testing Architecture

The testing strategy is **compile-only**: each Pascal unit is compiled individually to ensure it has no syntax errors and that its `uses` clauses are resolvable. There are no runtime unit tests.

### 8.1 How it works

1. **`mktests.pas`** generates a set of stub programs in `tests/src/` - one for each unit.
   - Example stub (`tests/src/t_map.pas`):
     ```pascal
     program t_map;
     uses map;
     begin
     end.
     ```
2. **`tests.bat`** iterates over every unit, calling `tst.bat` for each.
3. **`tst.bat`** compiles both the real unit (`src/<unit>.pas`) and its stub (`tests/src/t_<unit>.pas`) into `tests/tpuexe/`.
4. If **both** compilations succeed, the unit is marked `STATUS: OK` in `tests.log`. Otherwise, `STATUS: FAIL` or `STATUS: SKIP` is recorded.

### 8.2 What the test suite catches

- Syntax errors in individual units.
- Missing or misspelled `uses` clauses.
- Name clashes between units.
- Missing external declarations (e.g. `fade.pas` and `palette.pas` declare `external` procedures that must be provided by the ASM objects).

### 8.3 What it does **not** catch

- Link-time errors (those are caught by `build.bat` / `debug.bat`).
- Runtime logic errors.
- Behavioral differences from the original C code.

The compile-test suite is intentionally lightweight so it can be run frequently while iterating on the port.

---

## 9. Build & Debug Architecture (Log Files)

Both `build.bat` and `debug.bat` produce **comprehensive log files** that capture every compiler invocation and its output.

| Log file | Produced by | Contents |
|----------|-------------|----------|
| `bld.log` | `build.bat` | Full release build transcript: ASM assembly, driver linking, every `TPC.EXE` invocation, final success/failure message. |
| `dbg.log` | `debug.bat` | Same as `bld.log` but for the debug build. |
| `tests.log` | `tests.bat` | One block per unit, with `STATUS: OK / FAIL / SKIP` lines. |
| `DBG.LOG` | (original project) | Additional debug output from the original toolchain. |

The logs are **append-only** within a single run: each invocation of `build.bat` deletes the old `bld.log` and starts fresh. This makes it easy to spot the first error in a long build chain.

---

## 10. Current State of the Pascal Code

> **WARNING: This project is a work in progress. The Pascal code does not compile cleanly yet.**

The repository represents a **near-complete translation** of the original C code, but several units still contain:

- **Compile errors** - undeclared identifiers, type mismatches, and missing `uses` clauses.
- **Renamed units** - some units have been renamed to avoid clashes with Turbo Pascal's standard library or to follow Pascal naming conventions. For example:
  - `graphics.pas` is a thin wrapper that re-exports the driver procedures.
  - `audtabl.pas` is named `AUDIENCE_TABLES` internally but the file is `audtabl.pas`.
  - `inttabl.pas` is named `INTRO_TABLES`.
  - `fametbl.pas` is named `FAME_TABLES`.
- **Clause inconsistencies** - a few `uses` clauses reference units that have been renamed or that do not yet exist. These must be corrected.
- **Incomplete units** - some procedures are stubs or contain `{ ... omitted for brevity }` comments where the original C code was particularly long (e.g. `find_slot` in `economy.pas`, `ai_order` in `unitai.pas`).
- **External dependencies** - units like `fade.pas` and `palette.pas` declare `external` procedures that are implemented in the ASM helpers. These will link correctly only after `asm.bat` has produced the corresponding `.OBJ` files.

**The code is therefore best treated as a high-quality skeleton** - the structure, types, and the vast majority of the logic are present, but a focused effort is needed to make it compile and link.

---

## 11. Using This Project with an AI Agent

Because the code is **structurally complete but not yet compilable**, it is an **ideal candidate for an AI coding agent**. The agent can:

- Fix the remaining compile errors unit by unit (using `tests.bat` as a feedback loop).
- Complete the stubbed-out procedures (`find_slot`, `ai_order`, etc.).
- Reconcile renamed units and correct `uses` clauses.
- Verify that the Pascal code matches the original C semantics.

**Recommended workflow:**

1. Feed the agent `conversion.txt` (the single-file snapshot) or the entire repository.
2. Ask the agent to run `tests.bat` and fix the first failing unit.
3. Repeat until `tests.bat` reports **0 failures**.
4. Run `build.bat` and fix any link-time errors.
5. Run the resulting `CIV.EXE` in DOSBox-X and compare behaviour with the original game.

The AI can also use the **MASM listing files** (`.LST`) and **cross-reference files** (`.CRF`) to understand the exact assembly semantics that the Pascal code must replicate (see [13. MASM in This Project](#13-masm-in-this-project)).

---

## 12. Generated Folders & Files

Running the batch files creates the following artefacts:

| Folder / File | Created by | Purpose |
|---------------|------------|---------|
| `obj/` | `asm.bat rel` | Release `.OBJ` files + `.LST` + `.CRF` |
| `dbg_obj/` | `asm.bat dbg` | Debug `.OBJ` files + `.LST` + `.CRF` |
| `build/` | `build.bat` | `CIV.EXE`, `CIV.OVR`, `MGRAPHIC.EXE`, `MISC.EXE`, `NSOUND.CVL`, copied data files |
| `dbg_bld/` | `debug.bat` | Same as `build/` but with debug symbols |
| `units/` | `build.bat` / `debug.bat` | Compiled `.TPU` unit files |
| `tests/src/` | `mktests.pas` | Generated compile-test stubs |
| `tests/tpuexe/` | `tests.bat` | Compiled `.TPU` / `.EXE` from the test suite |
| `bld.log` | `build.bat` | Release build log |
| `dbg.log` | `debug.bat` | Debug build log |
| `tests.log` | `tests.bat` | Compile-test results |
| `conversion.txt` | `collect.bat` | Single-file concatenation of the entire project |

> **Note:** `data/` is an *input*, not an output - it must be populated from the original game before `build.bat` can produce a runnable `civ.exe`. See [3. Restoring the Game Data](#3-restoring-the-game-data).

---

## 13. MASM in This Project

### 13.1 What MASM is used for

The project uses **MASM 5.10** to assemble six `.ASM` sources under `asm/`. These are the game's **low-level helpers** - the parts of the original game that were written in assembly for speed or direct hardware access, and that the Pascal code calls via `external` declarations.

| Source | What it becomes | Role |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `asm/resident.asm` | `obj/resident.obj` | INT 8 timer hook, palette fading, palette cycling, DOS overlay loader, driver dispatch |
| `asm/graphics.asm` | `obj/graphics.obj` | Rasterizer, picture codec, mouse glue, clipping |
| `asm/f0data.asm` | `obj/f0data.obj` | Initialized DGROUP data for the resident helpers |
| `asm/mgraphic.asm` | `obj/mgraphic.obj` -> `build/mgraphic.exe` | MCGA/VGA graphics driver |
| `asm/misc.asm` | `obj/misc.obj` -> `build/misc.exe` | Keyboard + joystick overlay |
| `asm/asound.asm` | `obj/asound.obj` -> `build/nsound.cvl` | OPL2 sound driver |

Each source is assembled **independently** by `asm.bat` (release) or `asm.bat dbg` (debug) - the only MASM step in the whole project. The Pascal compiler `TPC.EXE` does not need MASM to compile the Pascal units; MASM is only needed so the Pascal `external` declarations find their matching symbols at link time.

### 13.2 Files produced by the batch files

`asm.bat` invokes MASM with the classic four-slot syntax:

```
MASM.EXE <flags> source.asm, object.obj, listing.lst, xref.crf;
```

So each assembly file yields **three** normal outputs (plus one failure-only file):

| File | Content | Format | Produced by | In `asm.bat`? |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| `.OBJ` | Relocatable object - the input to `LINK.EXE` and `TPC.EXE` | **binary** (OMF) | `MASM.EXE` (slot 2) | yes |
| `.LST` | Assembly listing + symbol table + macro expansions + error summary | **plain text** | `MASM.EXE` (slot 3) | yes |
| `.CRF` | Raw cross-reference data - symbol names plus the line numbers where each is defined and used | **binary** | `MASM.EXE` (slot 4) | yes |
| `.ERR` | Error listing | plain text | `MASM.EXE` (auto) | only on failure |
| `.REF` | Human-readable cross-reference report | **plain text** | `CREF.EXE` | **not invoked** |

> **Note:** `.REF` is **not produced** by the current batch files. `asm.bat` stops at the binary `.CRF`. To get the readable `.REF`, run the standalone `CREF.EXE` utility that ships with MASM 5.10 once per module:
>
> ```bat
> %masmdir%\CREF.EXE %outdir%\resident.crf,%outdir%\resident.ref;
> ```
>
> Adding that line after each MASM invocation in `asm.bat` (and adding `*.ref` to the cleanup block and to `.gitignore`) is the recommended one-line change if you want cross-reference listings.

### 13.3 Binary vs text at a glance

| Readable in a text editor? | Files |
| :--- | :--- |
| **Yes - plain ASCII** | `.LST`, `.REF`, `.ERR`, `.MAP` |
| **No - binary data** | `.OBJ`, `.CRF`, `.EXE`, `.OVR`, `.CVL`, `.TPU`, `.@$@` |

The `.CRF` file is deliberately binary: it is a *data* file meant as input to `CREF.EXE`, not a document. Opening it in a text editor will show garbage. The readable equivalent is the `.REF` file, which the batch files do not currently generate.

### 13.4 Why each one matters for this port

- **`.LST` (text) - the single most useful file for the ASM <-> Pascal boundary.**
  For each ASM routine, the `.LST` records the exact symbol name (with or without the leading underscore), its storage class (`NEAR` / `FAR`), its segment, and the machine code MASM emitted. If a Pascal unit declares `procedure resident_init; far; external name '_resident_init';`, you verify all four facts against the `.LST`. It also shows every `PUBLIC` and `EXTRN` in the module, so it doubles as the "what can Pascal call?" reference.

- **`.CRF` (binary) - the raw material for `.REF`.**
  It contains, for every symbol in the module, its definition and its use sites. On its own it is unreadable; its only consumer is `CREF.EXE`. It is worth keeping as an archive input: if you ever want to regenerate a `.REF` without re-assembling, the `.CRF` is what you feed to `CREF`.

- **`.REF` (text) - the navigable cross-reference.**
  It answers *"where is `_sprite_draw` defined?"*, *"where is it referenced?"*, and *"which Pascal units depend on which ASM symbols?"* in a single pass. It is the most useful file for identifying dead code and for reconciling the Pascal `external` declarations against the actual ASM exports. **Not produced by the current batch files** - see the CREF note above.

- **`.ERR` (text) - quick failure inspection.**
  Appears only when assembly fails. `asm.bat` already redirects MASM's stdout to `bld.log` / `dbg.log`, so `.ERR` is a convenience: `type obj\resident.err` shows just the errors, without scrolling the build log.

### 13.5 Other useful MASM / LINK outputs

- **`.OBJ`** - the actual linker input; not human-readable, but essential.
- **`.MAP`** (produced by `LINK.EXE`, not MASM) - the segment and symbol map of the final `.EXE` / `.OVR` / `.CVL`. Useful for verifying memory layout and overlay placement. Produced by adding `/MAP` to the `LINK.EXE` command line in `linkdrv.bat`.
- **`.COD`** - produced by Microsoft C, **not** MASM. Only relevant if you ever compare the Pascal port against the original C build (the `.COD` is the C equivalent of MASM's `.LST`).

---

## 14. Target Environment

This project is **explicitly targeted at**:

- **Compiler:** Turbo Pascal 7.01 **or** Borland Pascal with Objects 7.01
- **Assembler:** Microsoft Macro Assembler (MASM) **5.10** (mandatory - later versions break byte-equivalence)
- **Operating System:** MS-DOS 6.22 (or a compatible DOS environment such as DOSBox-X)
- **CPU:** 8086 / 80286 / 80386 (the code is `.8086`-compatible, though `.186` and `.286` instructions are used in specific modules)

> **Why MS-DOS 6.22?** The original game was designed for MS-DOS, and the batch files, memory model, and overlay system all assume a real-mode DOS environment. Running under DOSBox-X provides the necessary floppy-disk emulation and timer accuracy.

---

## 15. Notes and Ideas

The author's working notes, lightly edited - the *why* behind the port, plus a grab-bag of ideas worth exploring.

### 15.1 Why Pascal, anyway?

The Microsoft C compiler vs. the Turbo/Borland Pascal compiler has been discussed at length, and the conclusion is that the Pascal toolchain is **simply easier to use**:

- The way it **links** and **does overlays** is straightforward.
- The 64 KB segment model *just works* - no need to hand-tune segment layout.
- Turbo Pascal 7.01 has a beautiful IDE, and `TDX` (Turbo Debugger 3.2) can step into assembly and into overlays.

Microsoft C gives finer control over segment vs. overlay loading - but at the cost of having to know the program's layout in advance. Pascal's 64 KB-based overlays trade a little flexibility for a **lot** of sanity. Linker problems bite you-know-where every time; Pascal/Delphi is the sane alternative, then and now.

### 15.2 The assembly is still being converted

The ASM helpers (`RESIDENT.ASM`, `GRAPHICS.ASM`, `MGRAPHIC.ASM`, `MISC.ASM`, `ASOUND.ASM`) are **already** byte-for-byte reproductions of the originals - they build with MASM 5.10 and LINK 5.01 exactly as the 1991 sources did. The eventual plan is to **eliminate the assembly entirely** and reimplement it in Pascal, because:

- Pascal can express the same logic more readably.
- Turbo Debugger can step through it at source level.
- A single-language project is easier to maintain - and easier to hand to an AI agent for completion.

For now, though, the `.ASM` files are the source of truth for the low-level behaviour (VGA DAC writes, the OPL2 sound driver, the INT 8 timer tick, the mouse driver glue, the EGA/VGA/MCGA graphics primitives). Keep them - they are the Rosetta Stone.

### 15.3 The C to Pascal operator table

When transcribing the remaining C code, apply these transformations consistently:

| C | Pascal |
|---|---|
| `&&` | `and` |
| `\|\|` | `or` |
| `!` | `not` |
| `^` (XOR) | `xor` - **beware**: `^` in Pascal is dereference! |
| `<<` / `>>` | `shl` / `shr` (C's `>>` on signed ints is arithmetic - matches Pascal `sar`) |
| `==` / `!=` | `=` / `<>` |
| `0x...` | `$...` |
| `struct.field` | `record.field` |
| `if (x) y;` | `if x then y;` |
| `for (i=0; i<n; i++)` | `for i := 0 to n - 1 do` |
| `switch` | `case ... of` |
| `char*` | `PChar` (TP7 has no `const` strings) |
| Pointer arithmetic | `Ptr(seg, ofs)` or typed pointers |

### 15.4 Ideas worth exploring

- **Replace the inline `DB`-opcode blocks with real instructions.** Several ASM functions use `DB 081H,0ECH,...` (raw opcode bytes) to reproduce the exact byte sequence MASM 5.10 would emit. If you use a different assembler or change flags, those blocks are the *only* way to preserve byte equivalence - but they hurt readability. Keep them in `asm/` as-is and mirror the logic in readable Pascal on the ported side.

- **Unit-rename audit.** A `grep`-driven audit of `uses` clauses will flush out any inconsistencies introduced by the renames (`graphics.pas` wrapper, `audtabl.pas` = `AUDIENCE_TABLES`, `inttabl.pas` = `INTRO_TABLES`, `fametbl.pas` = `FAME_TABLES`, ...). `tests.bat` will then verify them.

- **Fill in the stubbed procedures.** `find_slot` (economy.pas), `ai_order` (unitai.pas), and the discovery-menu loop in `reduce_attitude` are the biggest stubs. The original C is right next door in `sjmelia/civd` - transcribe verbatim, apply the operator table above, and let `tests.bat` confirm it compiles.

- **The `$8F`-glyph trick.** Many string literals in the Pascal code contain `#$8F`, `#$8C`, `#$87`, `#$83`, `#$84` - these are **code-page characters** that render as arrows, underlines, or bullet points in the DOS CP437 font. Keep them; they *are* the intended output.

- **`conversion.txt` for AI agents.** `collect.bat` produces a single-file snapshot of the entire project (all `.bat`, `.pas`, `.asm`, `.inc`). This is *fantastic* for feeding to an AI agent - one file, complete context, no `git` tooling required. It is regenerated on demand and **ignored** by git (see `.gitignore`) because it is a build artifact; use `git add -f conversion.txt` if you want to ship a frozen snapshot.

- **MASM `.CRF` and `.LST` as reverse-engineering aids.** The assembler produces these alongside the `.OBJ` files. `.LST` gives you the exact machine code, symbol table, and macro expansions - essential when writing Pascal `external` declarations. `.CRF` gives you the cross-reference data; feed it to `CREF.EXE` to get a readable `.REF`. Together they make the ASM <-> Pascal boundary fully inspectable.

- **`TPX.EXE` vs `TDX.EXE` for development.** `TPX.EXE` is the lightweight protected-mode IDE - faster to boot, plenty of memory. `TDX.EXE` (Turbo Debugger 3.2) is the heavyweight: it can step **into assembly** and **into overlay code**. Use `TPX` for day-to-day editing and `TDX` for deep debugging.

- **DOSBox-X, not vanilla DOSBox.** The `IMGMOUNT` + "Swap Disk" workflow is far more reliable than manual floppy swapping when installing TP/BP from the original 3.5" images.

- **Running the batch files from Windows 11.** The batch files could be improved so that they run directly from Windows 11, rather than only from inside DOSBox-X. If they were runnable from Windows, advanced AI agents (usually 32-bit or 64-bit, running natively in Windows, or web-based agents with "computer use" control) could drive the build loop more easily. Most agents will probably never run inside DOSBox-X.

- **Capturing MS-DOS console output via DOSBox-X.** Perhaps the MS-DOS console output of the tools can be captured by DOSBox-X itself, for even better logging. MASM 5.01 writes directly to screen/`CON` and cannot be captured via pipes or redirects (it does not use `stdio`), so DOSBox-X's screen-capture facility could fill exactly that gap.

### 15.5 A nostalgic aside

Back in 1990 `TDX.EXE` was a bit too advanced to fully grasp. Today it's genuinely interesting to go back and try out these "advanced futures of the time": protected mode, 64 KB overlays, real source-level debugging into assembly. Both `TPX` and `TDX` remind me of early Delphi - and `TDX` especially feels like it was integrated into Delphi later on. :)

The batch-file quirks are part of that nostalgia too: MASM 5.01 writes directly to the screen/`CON` and cannot be captured via pipes or redirects (it does not use `stdio`), so its output goes to the console while the rest goes to `build.log`. Historical inconvenience, preserved in amber.

### 15.6 The bottom line

The Pascal code is *almost* there. The structure, the types, the vast majority of the logic, and all the low-level glue are in place. What remains is a focused completion pass - unit by unit, guided by `tests.bat` and cross-referenced against the original C. This is exactly the sort of task an AI agent can now do well, given `conversion.txt` and a clear success criterion ("zero failures in `tests.bat`").

Now you can prepare yourself for what is to come! =D

---

## 16. References

- **Original C decompilation:** [sjmelia/civd](https://github.com/sjmelia/civd)
- **This Pascal port:** [SkybuckFlying/Civ1Pas](https://github.com/SkybuckFlying/Civ1Pas)
- **CivFanatics development thread:** [Skybuck's Civilization 1 for Turbo Pascal 7.01 / Borland Pascal 7.01](https://forums.civfanatics.com/threads/skybucks-civilization-1-for-turbo-pascal-7-01-borland-pascal-7-01.705217/)
- **Turbo Pascal 7.0 Language Guide:** [PDF](https://turbopascal.org/wp-content/uploads/Turbo_Pascal_Version_7.0_Language_Guide_1992.pdf)
- **MASM 5.0 Programmer's Guide:** [PDF](https://dn721802.ca.archive.org/0/items/bitsavers_microsoftm1987410610014500R000787MASM5.0Programmer_54026053/410610014-500-R00-0787_MASM_5.0_Programmers_Guide_198707.pdf)

  - [Turbo Pascal 7.01](https://winworldpc.com/product/turbo-pascal/7x)
  - [Borland Pascal 7.01](https://winworldpc.com/product/borland-pascal)
  - [MASM 5.1](https://winworldpc.com/product/macro-assembler/5x)

# Skunny: Back to the Forest — a measured directory

A byte-level documentation of one installed MS-DOS game directory: twenty
files, 2,097,032 bytes, Copysoft / Edisys sc, Brussels, © 1993, shareware
version 1.0. **No product bytes are in this repository** — hashes, formats,
figures and the commands that reproduce them are.

## The short sheet

| | |
| --- | --- |
| object | `Skunny: Back to the Forest`, Copysoft, MS-DOS |
| year | **1993**, read off `ORDERP23.PCX` in pixels — no string in the object states it |
| medium | **none.** A directory on a hard disc, for the second object running |
| files | 20, 2,097,032 bytes, 20 distinct sha1 |
| archives | five `.LID`, 1,804,320 bytes, **221 members**, residue 0 on 5 of 5 |
| denominators | **D1 = 2,097,032** (the files) · **D2 = 2,092,060** (members + non-archives) |
| coverage | **D1 73.1869 %** · D2 73.1232 % |
| of which | **47.5675 points are `.PCX`**, a published ZSoft specification — 65 % of everything identified. Without it, 25.6194 % |
| provenance | **ten distinct mtimes**, the first surviving dates in five objects: copied 2016-06-24, played 2020-06-13 at 22:41 |
| third parties | Borland C++ · `WORX TOOLKIT 2.01(A)`, Mystic Software 1993 · LZEXE 0.91 in `INSTALL.COM` |
| symbol tables | **433 and 891 identifiers**, un-stripped, 349 shared, parsed to residue 0 |
| personal data | one name, published: **Philippe Mercier, Chairman, Copysoft**, drawn in pixels on an order screen. **None** in either symbol table. **None** in the high-score file, whose six name fields are 120 bytes of spaces |
| predictions | 54 clauses written first; inherited **11.50 of 13**, open **29.35 of 41** |

## The chapters

| | |
| --- | --- |
| [00](docs/00-predictions.md) | predictions — 54 clauses, written before anything was opened |
| [01](docs/01-the-object.md) | the object — what it is, two denominators, what it keeps and loses |
| [02](docs/02-the-technical-sheet.md) | the technical sheet — every figure with the command that remakes it |
| [03](docs/03-the-container.md) | the container — an archive with no magic, a dirty buffer, a member stored twice |
| [04](docs/04-the-pictures.md) | the pictures — somebody else's specification, and the year it put on the screen |
| [05](docs/05-the-sprites.md) | the sprites — a chain of banks, eight tables, and a pairing that was wrong |
| [06](docs/06-the-levels.md) | the levels — a grid whose height two different files agree on |
| [07](docs/07-the-sound.md) | the sound — a negative right about the bytes and wrong about the conclusion |
| [08](docs/08-the-programs.md) | the programs — what is left to measure when the binary names its own variables |
| [09](docs/09-the-user-state.md) | the user state and the dates — the first object in five whose provenance survived |
| [10](docs/10-against-the-collection.md) | against the collection — zero over two roots, two corrections to send |
| [11](docs/11-skunny-kart.md) | Skunny Kart — the cross this object can run, and the one it cannot |
| [12](docs/12-corrections.md) | corrections — eight of mine, six of the pre-briefing's, six inherited defects |
| [13](docs/13-leftovers.md) | leftovers — what stayed closed, with a byte count on each |
| [14](docs/14-prediction-scoring.md) | prediction scoring — and a twelfth calibration entry at −3.40 |

## The formats, all measured here

**`.LID`** — no magic, no count field. A directory of 22-byte records
(14-byte name, `u32` size, `u32` offset) whose length is recovered because
`offsets[0] == 22 × entries`, terminated by a NUL-leading record, chain
contiguous, residue 0 on 5 of 5. The name field is an **uncleared buffer**:
66 of 221 members carry the tail of their predecessor.

**`S*` sprite banks** — a member is a chain of banks; each bank is a 12-byte
header (`u16 w`, `u16 h`, `u16 frames`, 6 unnamed bytes) followed by
`frames × w × h` bytes of flat 8-bit raster. 78 members walk to EOF with
residue 0. Where a member has two banks, the second is the first **mirrored**:
34 of 34 are closer to the mirror of bank 0 than to bank 0 itself.

**`RACE.L*`** — eight index tables, `u16 count` then 32-byte records of an
18-byte label, a 10-byte resource stem and two `u16`. The identity
`member size == payload + 12 × banks` holds on **59 of the 59** records that
name a bank, measured from two files at once.

**`RACE.?M`** — flat `w × 13` grids of one-byte tile indices into `F1.SBL`'s
126-frame tileset; every byte of all seven is a valid index, and the 13 is
independently stated by `RACE.GAM`.

**`.VCE`** — `u16` rate, `u16` flag, then a Creative VOC **block chain with no
26-byte file header**, closing 12 of 12. The twelve extracted WAVs were played
back and confirmed correct by the owner of the machine.

**`.BPR`** — `FF FF FF FF`, `n` six-byte records of three `u16` where the third
is an 8253 timer divisor, an `FF` terminator, `len == 5 + 6n` on 12 of 12.
100.0 Hz to 4,100 Hz. **A tone list, not pulse-width modulation** — which
settles an open cross-object comparison in the negative.

**`AUDIO.INS`** — 128 × 16 OPL2 instrument bank, confirmed by three range
tests at 128 of 128.

**`.MKB`**, **`.MBI`**, **`FONT1.INF`**, **`.PAL`**, **`HI.TBL`** — each closes
on one line of arithmetic; see chapters 06 and 09.

**Borland symbol tables** — `0x52FB`, name-pool length at `+4`, pool at the end
of the region, walked to residue 0 on 2 of 2, with the header's own count
agreeing and its declared image size matching the MZ header at the other end
of the file.

## What is not in this repository

The twenty files of the product, any member extracted from them, any rendered
image, any extracted sound, and `_work\`. The `.gitignore` excludes the object
directory outright and every product extension by name.

## Tools

`tools/` holds 436 Python files: 426 inherited from
`pc-linksthechallengeofgolf-doc` and **ten written here** — `lid.py`,
`pcx.py`, `sbank.py`, `ltab.py`, `vce.py`, `bpr.py`, `tds.py`, `sbi.py`,
`mkb.py`, `gamedata.py` — plus `account.py`, rewritten. Every one of them
prints how many files it opened out of how many it was given and exits
non-zero when that number is short.
