# TRAUMA – First Demo (19.05.1991) The first production of the group **Trauma**, released on **19 May 1991**: code by **The Beast 666**, graphics by **Critter**, music by **DeathJester**. The scrolltext says it was coded in two weeks, "half hour a day", just after The Beast 666 and Critter left Resolution 101 Italy to join Trauma. Cyberbit, another member, writes the middle of it.

The demo has three parts: 1. **Opening, about 1:40.** Eleven lines of text, one at a time: "We've done it another time !", "Only for your pleasure !!!", "A new COOL group is born ...", up to "TRAUMA, a new way to be COOL!", the credits and "Release Date: 19.05.1991". Each line slides down from the top of the screen to the middle, stays there about 4 seconds, then slides on into the white lower half, where it fades out. The music starts here and plays through the whole demo. 2. **Main part, until the left mouse button.** The TRAUMA logo at the top, a parallax star field, a 4-bitplane scroller at the bottom, and in the middle two things that take turns: **text pages** that scroll up line by line (credits, the group's BBS list, the member list, a contact page, a call for members), and a **3D cube of 20 balls** that rotates and moves towards and away from the viewer. 3. **End part.** A one-bitplane text scroller with the credits and the greetings. The right mouse button pauses it, the left one returns to the CLI. ## Contents of the repository | Path | What it is | |---|---| | [TRAUMA-FirstDemo 19.05.91](TRAUMA-FirstDemo%2019.05.91) | the original executable, packed | | [TRAUMA-FirstDemo 19.05.asm](TRAUMA-FirstDemo%2019.05.asm), [.cnf](TRAUMA-FirstDemo%2019.05.cnf) | IRA disassembly of the original executable (depacker + packed data) | | [work/trauma.asm](work/trauma.asm) | **relocatable rebuild** of the whole demo, assembles with vasm | | [work/Makefile](work/Makefile) | build, check and run targets | | [work/unpacked_30000.asm](work/unpacked_30000.asm), [.cnf](work/unpacked_30000.cnf) | raw IRA disassembly of the unpacked image at `$30000`, with the config that names code areas and labels | | [work/decrunch.py](work/decrunch.py) | depacker in Python; recreates the unpacked image from the original file | | [work/checkreloc.py](work/checkreloc.py) | used by `make verify` to look for addresses left as numbers | | [work/extract_assets.py](work/extract_assets.py) | extracts the assets | | [work/assets/](work/assets) | the extracted assets (see [Assets](#assets)) | | [docs/screenshots/](docs/screenshots) | screenshots from the tests | ## Build and run You need [vasm](http://sun.hasenbraten.de/vasm/) (`vasmm68k_mot`), `exe2adf`, Python 3 (with Pillow for the assets) and FS-UAE. ```sh cd work make # trauma (AmigaDOS executable) + trauma.adf (bootable disk) make verify # see "How it was checked" make assets # unpacks the original and extracts the assets make run # FS-UAE: A500, KS 1.3, 512K chip + 512K slow make run600 # FS-UAE: A600, KS 2.05, 1MB chip (stock) make run1200 # FS-UAE: A1200, KS 3.1, 2MB chip, no fast RAM ``` To get the unpacked image back from the original file: ```sh python3 work/decrunch.py "TRAUMA-FirstDemo 19.05.91" unpacked_30000.bin ``` ## Testing All tests were done in FS-UAE 3.1.66. Each run went through the whole demo: the opening, about a minute of the main part (pages and cube), the left mouse button, the end part, the left mouse button again, and then a command typed into the shell. | Machine | Original | Rebuild | |---|---|---| | A500: 68000, OCS, KS 1.3, 512K chip + 512K slow | works | works, clean return to the shell | | A500: same, 512K chip only | not tested | works, clean return to the shell | | A600: 68000, ECS, KS 2.05, 1MB chip | *Software Failure 8000 000B* a few seconds after the first line of text, every time | works, clean return to the shell | | A1200: 68020, AGA, KS 3.1, 2MB chip | runs, but each opening line stays on screen a third of the time; after the exit the screen stays black and the shell does not come back | works, clean return to the shell | | A1200: same + 4MB fast RAM | not tested | works, clean return to the shell | | CD32: 68020, AGA, KS 3.1 (40.60), booted from a CD with only the demo | not tested | works, clean return to the shell | | CD32, started from the ItaloDisco 4 menu (F8) of [Stage-Swaptro](https://github.com/Ozzyboshi/Stage-Swaptro) | works in FS-UAE, by luck; with 8 KB more chip RAM in use at boot, *Software Failure 8000 0004* right after the unpacking (on a real CD32 it reboots there) | works, also with the 8 KB more in use; after the exit the menu reboots as it is meant to | Why the original fails is explained in [Why the original crashes](#why-the-original-crashes). ## The packed executable The original file is 116,240 bytes. It has two hunks: a code hunk of 116,180 bytes, which holds a small depacker followed by the packed data, and a 4-byte BSS hunk that is never used. There are no relocations: the depacker uses PC-relative addressing only, and the destination is an absolute address. ### Depacker The depacker (`$32250`–`$32338` in [the disassembly](TRAUMA-FirstDemo%2019.05.asm)) is followed by a 12-byte header: | Offset | Value | Meaning | |---|---|---| | +0 | `$0001C4E0` | size of the packed stream (115,936 bytes) | | +4 | `$00036000` | size of the unpacked image (221,184 bytes) | | +8 | `$14363290` | checksum: XORed with every longword of the stream, it gives 0 | This is the **ByteKiller** format. The stream is read **backwards**, one longword at a time, and the output is written backwards too, from `$30000+$36000` = `$66000` down to `$30000`. Bits are taken from the low end of `D0` with `LSR.L #1`; when `D0` becomes zero the next longword is loaded and shifted with `ROXR.L #1` after `MOVE #$10,CCR` has set X, which puts a 1 in bit 31 as an end marker. While it works, the depacker copies `$DFFA06` to `COLOR00` (probably a mirror of `VHPOSR`), which makes the screen flash. At the end it jumps to `$30000`. It computes the checksum but never checks it. | Code | Meaning | |---|---| | `0 0` + 3 bits *n* | *n*+1 literal bytes (1–8) | | `0 1` + 8 bits | copy 2 bytes, 8-bit offset | | `1 00` + 9 bits | copy 3 bytes, 9-bit offset | | `1 01` + 10 bits | copy 4 bytes, 10-bit offset | | `1 10` + 8 bits *n* + 12 bits | copy *n*+1 bytes (1–256), 12-bit offset | | `1 11` + 8 bits *n* | *n*+9 literal bytes (9–264) | The bytes of a copy are taken from `dest + offset`, one at a time. [decrunch.py](work/decrunch.py) follows the 68000 code step by step; the checksum gives 0 and the stream is used up exactly when the output reaches `$30000`, which confirms the decoding. The depacker writes to `$30000`–`$66000` **without allocating that memory**, and the demo then uses `$70000`–`$7FFFF` as screen memory, again without allocating it. ### Why the original crashes Writing over memory that belongs to someone else works only if nothing important happens to be there. Whether it is depends on the machine, the Kickstart and what was loaded before: - **The packed file itself.** On a machine with only chip RAM (CD32, A1200 without fast RAM) the 116 KB hunk is loaded into chip RAM, often low enough to overlap `$30000`–`$66000`. Since the output is written backwards, the depacker survives only if its own code and the start of the packed stream lie below `$30000`. A simulation of the depacker with the hunk at different addresses shows that the unpacked image is correct only if the hunk starts at `$2FF08` or lower (or wholly above `$66000`); above that, the output overwrites packed data that has not been read yet. Started from the ItaloDisco menu on a CD32 in FS-UAE, the hunk is at `$2E5B8`: 6,480 bytes of margin. With 8 KB more chip RAM in use at boot it lands at `$31008`, the image comes out wrong, and the jump to `$30000` ends in *Software Failure 8000 0004* (illegal instruction). A real CD32 with a slightly different boot is enough to cross the line, and there the crash shows up as a reboot after the unpacking. - **The stack of the CLI.** On the A600 with KS 2.05 the hunk is at `$17088`, well below `$30000`, and the image unpacks correctly. But the stack of the CLI process is at `$346F4`, inside the image. The first instruction of the unpacked demo is `MOVEM.L D1-D7/A0-A6,-(A7)`: it writes 56 bytes over the music player (`$344A4`–`$34FEC`), and when the music starts the CPU runs into garbage: *Software Failure 8000 000B*. - **Everything else** in `$30000`–`$66000` and `$70000`–`$7FFFF` (buffers, other programs, the selector of a menu) is overwritten too. The rebuild is a normal executable: the hunk loader puts it wherever there is room and fixes the addresses, and the screen memory is a BSS hunk, so none of this can happen. ## Memory map of the unpacked image | Address | Size | Content | |---|---|---| | `$30000` | 4 | `BRA.W $30200` | | `$30010` | 368 | hidden note from the author (see [Texts](#texts)) | | `$30200` | | code: start, system, part 1 | | `$30722` | | part 1 data: font offsets, the 11 lines of text | | `$30928` | | part 2 code | | `$31600` | | part 2 data: variables, font offsets, the six text pages (`$31768`), the scrolltext (`$31FEA`), sine and cosine tables (`$32C4C`, `$32F1C`, 360 words each), state of the cube (`$331EC`), work arrays, the 20 points of the cube (`$33606`) | | `$33680` | | part 3 code, end text (`$339C0`) | | `$344A4` | | ProTracker replay and its data, up to `$355E2` | | `$355E2` | 4 | `$000003F2`: the HUNK_END of the original executable | | `$355E6` | | empty, up to `$40000` | | `$40000` | 131,028 | ProTracker module "algorhythmic" | | `$60000` | 4 × 2,200 | logo, 320×55, 4 bitplanes one after the other | | `$62260` | 7,680 | scroller font | | `$64060` | 3,000 | font of parts 1 and 3 | | `$64C18` | 4,680 | font of the text pages | | `$65E60` | 96 + 96 | ball, 3 bitplanes, and its mask | | `$65F20` | | empty, up to `$66000` | The HUNK_END at `$355E2` shows how the demo was put together: the code was assembled with DevPac as a normal program, then the module and the graphics were loaded at fixed addresses (`$40000`, `$60000`), and the whole memory area from `$30000` to `$66000` was packed. At run time the parts build their copper lists and screens in `$70000`–`$7FFFF`: | Address | Content | Name in the rebuild | |---|---|---| | `$70000` | copper list of the current part | `Copper` | | `$70500` | sprite 0: the star field | `Stars` | | `$70800` | sprites 1–7 (empty) | `NullSprite` | | `$71CD8` | scroller, 4 bitplanes interleaved, 42 bytes per row | `ScrollPlanes` | | `$72800` | parts 1 and 3: one bitplane, 40 bytes per row | `TextPlane` | | `$73102`, `$79D02` | the two screens of the middle area, 3 bitplanes interleaved, 48 bytes per row | `BobScreenA`, `BobScreenB` | | `$78B02` | where the lines of the text pages are drawn | `PageText` | ## How the demo works ### Start-up and exit The code at `$30200` saves the registers, points the `TRAP #0` vector (`$80`) to `SuperMain`, and executes `TRAP #0`: **the whole demo runs in supervisor mode**, on the system stack, inside the trap handler. `SuperMain` calls `SysInit`, the three parts and `SysExit`, and ends with `RTE`. - `SysInit`: `Forbid()`, `OpenLibrary("graphics.library")`, `mt_init` with the module at `$40000`, saves `DMACON` and `INTENA`, clears `INTENA`, `INTREQ` and `ADKCON`, installs its level 3 handler at `$6C` and enables only the vertical blank interrupt. - `Level3Int` calls the music player and clears the interrupt request. It is used in parts 1 and 3. In part 2 every interrupt is off and the main loop calls the player itself, once per frame. - `SysExit`: stops the music, restores the vector, `DMACON`, `INTENA` and the system copper list (`gb_copinit`), `CloseLibrary()`, `Permit()`. All the code keeps `A0` = `$DFF000`. ### Part 1 The copper list has one bitplane. The top half of the screen is black and the bottom half is white (`COLOR00` changes at line `$AB`); `COLOR01`, the colour of the text, gets lighter in steps over lines `$39`–`$55`, and again from black to white over lines `$E3`–`$FF`. For each of the 11 lines, `P1Print` clears the bitplane and draws the text centred at its top, one character at a time with the blitter (11 pixels per character, `BLTCON0` = `$0BFA`, minterm A OR C). The display window is set to lines `$2A`–`$39`, and `DiwOpen` moves both `DIWSTRT` and `DIWSTOP` down by one line per frame: since the bitplane pointer does not change, the line of text slides down the screen. It stops at line `$A4`, in the middle, stays for 206 frames (on a 68000, see the fixes), then slides on to line `$FF`, into the white half where its colour fades to white, and stays 20 frames more. ### Part 2 The copper list, from top to bottom: - the logo, 4 bitplanes, 55 lines, that fades in at the start; - a blue and a red line made of `COLOR00` changes; - the middle area, 3 bitplanes, double buffered: the copper list points to the screen that is not being drawn; - another blue and red line; - the scroller, 4 bitplanes interleaved, below line 255. Sprite 0 is reused down the screen for a **star field**: 26 rows of three stars, 78 in all, each one line high, that move right by 2, 4 or 6 pixels per frame. Sprites 1–7 point to an empty sprite. The main loop waits for line `$12A` and runs once per frame (in FS-UAE it never needs more than one frame, on the A500 too). It moves the scroller, calls the music player, and then does one of two things: **Text pages** (`Mode` = 0). One of the six pages scrolls up into the middle area: every frame the blitter moves the area up by one row, and every 13 frames a new line of 30 characters is drawn at the bottom (the font is 13 rows high). Then the page stays for 700 frames (14 s), and the area fades out over 160 frames. The page font has 3 bitplanes and its colours are greens. The colours of the stars fade in and out with the pages. **The cube** (`Mode` = 1), for 500 frames (10 s). 20 balls placed on a 3×3×3 lattice, without the centre of each face and the centre of the cube: - `RotateObject` adds 2 degrees per frame to each of the three angles; - `ZoomObject` moves the cube towards and away from the viewer, between –200 and +200, by one unit per frame; - `Project3D` rotates the points around the three axes with the sine and cosine tables and `MULS`, then divides by the depth; - `SortZ` sorts the balls by depth (insertion sort), so that `DrawBobs` can draw them from back to front; - `ClearBobScreen` clears the screen with the blitter, and `DrawBobs` draws each ball with a masked blit (A = mask, B = ball, C = background, D = screen, minterm `$CA`). Then `Mode` goes back to 0 and the next page comes. **The scroller** uses a 16×16 font with 4 bitplanes. Every frame one blit moves the whole scroller left, in descending mode, with the shift taken from the speed; a new character is drawn every 16 pixels. In the text, `S` followed by a digit sets the speed (`S1`, `S2`, `S4` pixels per frame), and `$FF` starts the text again. The left mouse button ends the part: the logo, the middle area and the scroller fade out. ### Part 3 The same copper list as part 1, with a taller display window. Every 15 frames a new line of 29 characters is drawn at row 213 (the font is 15 rows high), and every frame the blitter moves the bitplane up by one row, so the text scrolls up and fades into the white half. When the text ends it starts again. The right mouse button pauses it: the code is `BTST #10,$DFF016`, a bit number above 7 on a memory byte, which the 68000 takes modulo 8; IRA does not accept it, so it is kept as data. The left button exits. ## Music "**algorhythmic**" by DeathJester: a 31-sample ProTracker module (`M.K.`), 131,028 bytes, 13 samples, 43 patterns, 47 positions, about 6 minutes before it loops. The sample names are the composer's comments: `#deathjester!!!`, `preliminary release`, `april 14th 1991`, `low sinister bass hum`, `nifty pong sound`, `overused cliche synth`, `middle eastern string`, `hark! a snare!`, `'tis a bassdrum, yes?`, `electropizzicatto` and others. The player is the standard ProTracker replay (`mt_init`, `mt_music`, `mt_end`). Like most players of the time, `mt_init` clears the first longword of every sample, the empty ones at the end included, so it writes 4 bytes just after the module; here they fall in the padding before `$60000`. ## Texts All in [work/assets/](work/assets): - [part1_texts.txt](work/assets/part1_texts.txt): the 11 lines of the opening. - [pages.txt](work/assets/pages.txt): the six text pages. The first one has the credits; then the BBS list (Power House 713-944-5162, Smuggler's Cove 908-527-8850, Vertigo 813-831-8466, Panic Zone 508-234-2150, Fantasy ++39-(0)832-350350), the member list (Assimilator, Cyberbit, Critter, DeathJester, Deathlok, Fashion Light, Lucky Lawa, Marko, Nemesis, Oddwunn, The Beast 666, Trillion, White Ninja), a page to contact The Beast 666, "only coders !!" (Andrea Epicoco, Via Pacinotti 51, 72023 Mesagne (BR), Italy, phone ++39-(0)831-730286, "3 pm - 4 pm or 21 pm - 22 pm") and a call for coders, graphicians and musicians. In the pages font the capital letters are decorations: "AA trauma AA" shows as a decorated "trauma". - [scrolltext.txt](work/assets/scrolltext.txt): the scroller of part 2. The Beast 666 says that the demo was made in two weeks, that he and Critter left Resolution 101 Italy for Trauma, and apologises to Storm and Sledge of Divina because the Resolution 101 megademo, and with it their "Vogue demo" with Divina's music, was never released. Then Cyberbit greets a long list of groups, and The Beast 666 closes: "this is my last school year ... you will be shocked when my next demo will be released (maybe, at smau '91 - milan - italy)". - [endtext.txt](work/assets/endtext.txt): part 3, the credits and the greetings of The Beast 666 & Critter and of Fashion Light (Skid Row, Agile, FairLight, The Company, Divina, SpellJammers, Razor 1911, Classic, DefJam, Vogue, C.a.b.a.l., Endless Piracy and others). - [author_note.txt](work/assets/author_note.txt): a note at `$30010`, framed by asterisks, that the code never shows: *"This demo was coded in DevPac 2.08 by The Beast 666 of Trauma. - 12.05.1991 - All my routines are 100% made by me, so don't rip them. If you want a cool production made by me call: ++39-(0)831-730286 or write a letter: Andrea Epicoco - Via Pacinotti, 51 - 72023 Mesagne (BR) - Italy. Good searching !!!!!"* ## Assets All in [work/assets/](work/assets): | File | Content | |---|---| | `algorhythmic.mod` | the music, ready to play in any ProTracker player | | `logo.png` | the TRAUMA logo, 320×55, 16 colours (signed "CRITTER" at the bottom right) | | `font_text.png` | font of parts 1 and 3, 1 bitplane, enlarged 2× | | `font_scroller.png` | scroller font, 16×16, 16 colours, enlarged 2× | | `font_pages.png` | font of the text pages, 8 colours, enlarged 2× | | `ball.png` | the ball of the cube, 16×16, with its mask, enlarged 8× | | `palettes.txt` | the colours of the logo, the scroller, the pages and the balls | | `cube.txt` | the 20 points of the cube | | `part1_texts.txt`, `pages.txt`, `scrolltext.txt`, `endtext.txt`, `author_note.txt` | the texts (see [Texts](#texts)) | ## The relocatable rebuild [work/trauma.asm](work/trauma.asm) is the whole unpacked image as vasm source, with no `ORG`: - every absolute address is a label: the routines, the variables, the texts, `MtModule`, `Logo`, the fonts, `BobGfx`, `BobMask`; - the code and the tables (`$30000`–`$355E6`) are a `CODE` section, which can go to any memory; the module and the graphics are two `DATA_C` sections, because the audio and the blitter must reach them; the 43 KB of zeros between the end of the program and the module (`$355E6`–`$40000`) are dropped; - the screen memory at `$70000`–`$7FFFF` is a 64 KB `BSS_C` section, `Buf`, and the areas inside it have names (`Copper`, `Stars`, `TextPlane`, …) with the same offsets as in the original. The hard part is that the original never handles these addresses as longwords. It builds its copper lists with immediate longwords like `MOVE.L #$00E00007,(A1)+` / `MOVE.L #$00E22800,(A1)+` (`BPL1PT` = `$72800`), and it sets the blitter pointers one word at a time: the high word is a constant (`MOVEQ #7,D0`, `MOVE.W #$0006,80(A0)`) and the low word is computed with 16-bit arithmetic from tables of low words (`BobScreenOffs`, `BobCopperOffs`, the font offsets). The hunk loader can only relocate whole longwords, so in the rebuild: - the copper pointers are written by the macro `COPPTR`, which splits the address at run time; - the blitter pointers are built as longwords: base address (`LEA TextPlane,A4`, `LEA Font1,A5`, `LEA Buf,A6` …) plus the original offset, then written with `MOVE.L`. The tables keep their values, which are now offsets from `Buf` or from a font instead of low words. Offsets that can go above `$7FFF` are extended without the sign. ### How it was checked Every block that had to change keeps the original instructions in an `IFD ORIGINAL` part. `make verify` does two things: 1. it assembles the source with `-DORIGINAL` at `ORG $30000` (and `Buf` at `$70000`): the result must be **identical to the unpacked image, byte for byte**; 2. it assembles it again at `$130000` (and `Buf` at `$170000`) and compares the two: every difference must be the high word of an address (207 of them). [checkreloc.py](work/checkreloc.py) also scans the source, outside the `ORIGINAL` parts, for numbers that look like addresses of the image or of the buffer, for copper moves that hold the high half of a pointer, and for constant high or low words written to the blitter pointers. Any of these would not be relocated, and the check fails. Then the rebuild was run on all the machines in [Testing](#testing). ### Memory | Hunk | Memory | Size | |---|---|---| | code and tables | any | 22,500 | | module | chip | 131,072 | | graphics | chip | 24,576 | | `Buf` (BSS) | chip | 65,536 | 238 KB in all, and no block bigger than the module. A first version of the rebuild kept the whole image in one chip hunk, as in the original: 287 KB, with a single block of 216 KB. On an A600 with no fast RAM and four hard disks mounted, the ItaloDisco menu rebooted at once when the demo was chosen, and without the hard disks it worked: most likely the filesystems took enough chip RAM that a 216 KB block was no longer free, and `LoadSeg()` failed (the menu reboots when a program does not load). In FS-UAE, with chip RAM taken up to leave 360 KB free at boot, the one-hunk version does not load and this one does. ### Bugs in the original and fixes These are fixed in the rebuild and marked `fix:` in the source. The `ORIGINAL` build still gives back the original code. | Bug | Effect | Fix | |---|---|---| | The depacker and the demo write to `$30000`–`$66000` and `$70000`–`$7FFFF` without allocating them | crashes on the A600 and on the CD32, see [Why the original crashes](#why-the-original-crashes) | normal relocatable executable, the screens in a `BSS_C` hunk | | The start code writes the `TRAP #0` vector at `$80` and the level 3 vector at `$6C` | on a 68010 or later the vectors are at `VBR`, which is not always 0 | `SuperMain` runs through exec `Supervisor()`; `VBR` is read with `MOVEC` when the CPU is a 68010 or later, and the level 3 vector is written at `VBR+$6C` | | `Forbid()`, `OpenLibrary()`, `CloseLibrary()` and `Permit()` are called in supervisor mode, inside the trap | the OS expects them from a task in user mode | the OS calls are made in user mode, before and after `Supervisor()` | | The OS view is left active | on AGA machines the display registers keep the values of the OS screen (`FMODE` …) | `LoadView(NULL)` and two `WaitTOF()` before starting; `FMODE` = `$0000`, `BPLCON3` = `$0C00`, `BPLCON4` = `$0011` (the OCS defaults; these registers do not exist on OCS/ECS); the old view is loaded back on exit | | `mt_music` saves `D0`–`D4`/`A0`–`A6` but uses `D7`, and `Level3Int` saves nothing | in parts 1 and 3 the music interrupt changes `D7` of the code it interrupts | `Level3Int` saves and restores every register, and clears `INTREQ` twice (on a 68040/060 one write can arrive after the `RTE`) | | `WaitFrames` calls a "wait for line ≥ `$10E`" routine `$A000` times | the routine returns at once below that line, so the delay depends on the CPU: 206 frames on a 68000, 63 on a 14 MHz 68020 (measured in FS-UAE); on the A1200 and the CD32 the opening lines flash by | waits whole frames, 1 for every 200 calls, which is the 68000 timing | | The player waits for the audio DMA with 300 `DBF` loops | about 6.5 scan lines on a 7 MHz 68000, much less on a faster CPU | waits for 7 changes of the beam line | | Most blits are started without waiting for the one before | with `BLTPRI` set, a 68000 running from chip RAM gets few bus cycles while the blitter works, and the timing happened to be enough; a faster CPU running from its cache can rewrite the blitter registers too early | `WaitBlit` before every blit, with the extra first read for the old Agnus | | `ADKCON` is cleared and never restored | the disk and audio settings of the OS are lost | saved and restored | On the A1200 the original does not come back to the shell after the exit; the rebuild does on every machine tested. I did not trace which of the problems above causes it. These are left as in the original: - the sine table holds `$8000` for sin 90° (and the cosine table for cos 0°): as a signed word that is –1.0 instead of +1.0. The code skips the rotation when an angle is 0, but when an angle is exactly 90°, once every 180 frames, the cube is drawn for one frame turned the other way on that axis; - the 4 bytes that `mt_init` clears after the module (harmless, they fall in the padding); - the busy waits on the beam position, which work on every CPU. ## Tools - [IRA](http://aminet.net/package/dev/asm/ira) 2.11, built from source, for the disassembly, with the config in [work/unpacked_30000.cnf](work/unpacked_30000.cnf) - [vasm](http://sun.hasenbraten.de/vasm/) and `exe2adf` for the build - FS-UAE 3.1.66 for the tests, and its debugger for the memory layout of the crashes - Python 3 + Pillow for the depacker, the checks and the asset extraction

# Dreams of Power – Born (1990) The intro that announced the Italian group **Dreams of Power** ("A NEW GROUP IS BORN !!!"), from Lugo (Ravenna). It was coded for them by **Reflex** of **Altered Brains**: the screen says *INTRO BY REFLEX* and *ALTERED BRAINS 1990*, and the scrolltext thanks "REFLEX / ALTERED BRAINS FOR THIS COOL INTRO". The music is "going strong", a ProTracker module made with samples from the ST sample disks.

Everything is on one screen, from top to bottom: - the **DREAMS OF POWER logo**, cut in two halves that swing sideways, each one on its own sine curve; - a **red sky and skyline**, made with copper colour changes and a one-bitplane silhouette; - three rows of **floppy disks** in parallax, moving at three different speeds; - a small **equalizer**: four lines whose length follows the four audio channels; - the **scroller**, with a 3-bitplane 32-pixel font, bent line by line into a wave. Its speed, the height and the length of the wave, and pauses, are set by commands inside the text. The left mouse button returns to the CLI. ## Contents of the repository | Path | What it is | |---|---| | [DreamsOfPower-Born](DreamsOfPower-Born) | the original executable, packed | | [DreamsOfPower-Born.asm](DreamsOfPower-Born.asm), [.cnf](DreamsOfPower-Born.cnf) | IRA disassembly of the original executable (depacker + packed data) | | [work/dreams.asm](work/dreams.asm) | **relocatable rebuild** of the whole intro, assembles with vasm | | [work/Makefile](work/Makefile) | build, check and run targets | | [work/dreams_unpacked](work/dreams_unpacked) | the program that the original executable unpacks: a normal AmigaDOS executable | | [work/dreams_unpacked.asm](work/dreams_unpacked.asm), [.cnf](work/dreams_unpacked.cnf) | raw IRA disassembly of it, with the config that names code areas and labels | | [work/data_55000.bin](work/data_55000.bin) | the graphics and the music, as the program unpacks them at `$55000`; the rebuild includes this file | | [work/decrunch.py](work/decrunch.py) | both depackers in Python; recreates `dreams_unpacked` and `data_55000.bin` from the original file | | [work/checkreloc.py](work/checkreloc.py), [work/hunkdata.py](work/hunkdata.py) | used by `make verify` | | [work/extract_assets.py](work/extract_assets.py) | extracts the assets | | [work/assets/](work/assets) | the extracted assets (see [Assets](#assets)) | | [docs/screenshots/](docs/screenshots) | screenshots from the tests | ## Build and run You need [vasm](http://sun.hasenbraten.de/vasm/) (`vasmm68k_mot`), `exe2adf`, Python 3 (with Pillow for the assets) and FS-UAE. ```sh cd work make # dreams (AmigaDOS executable) + dreams.adf (bootable disk) make verify # see "How it was checked" make assets # extracts the assets make run # FS-UAE: A500, KS 1.3, 512K chip + 512K slow make run600 # FS-UAE: A600, KS 2.05, 1MB chip (stock) make run1200 # FS-UAE: A1200, KS 3.1, 2MB chip, no fast RAM ``` To get the unpacked program and data back from the original file: ```sh python3 work/decrunch.py DreamsOfPower-Born dreams_unpacked data_55000.bin ``` ## Testing All tests were done in FS-UAE 3.1.66, booting a disk (or, for the CD32, a CD) whose startup-sequence runs the intro. Each run lasted about a minute and a half, then the left mouse button, then a command typed into the shell. | Machine | Original | Rebuild | |---|---|---| | A500: 68000, OCS, KS 1.3, 512K chip + 512K slow | runs; after the exit, *Guru Meditation #00000004* (illegal instruction) | works, clean return to the shell | | A500: same, 512K chip only | works | works, clean return to the shell | | A600: 68000, ECS, KS 2.05, 1MB chip | only the copper colours, no graphics (bitplane DMA is off, see below) | works, clean return to the shell | | A600: same, with three more floppy drives | same as above; started from the ItaloDisco menu, where DMA is on, it freezes with the logo half drawn and no scroller | works, clean return to the shell | | A1200: 68020, AGA, KS 3.1, 2MB chip | only the copper colours, no graphics | works, clean return to the shell | | A1200: same + 4MB fast RAM | only the copper colours, no graphics | works, clean return to the shell | | CD32: 68020, AGA, KS 3.1 (40.60), booted from a CD with only the intro | works | works, clean return to the shell | The Guru on the A500 with slow RAM comes right after the exit; I did not trace it, but the most likely cause is the memory at `$55000`–`$7E0B4` that the original overwrites and then clears without owning it. What goes wrong in the original is explained in [Bugs in the original](#bugs-in-the-original-and-fixes). ## The packed executable The original file is 77,836 bytes and has two hunks: a 524-byte code hunk with the depacker, and an 82,324-byte data hunk with the packed data. It is an *executable cruncher*: the packed data is a whole AmigaDOS executable, and the header does what `LoadSeg()` would do with it. 1. The packed stream is unpacked inside the data hunk, at offset `$200`. The format is the one of **PowerPacker**: the stream is read backwards, a 32-bit bit buffer is refilled from the end, and matches use offsets of 9, 10, 11 or 11 bits (the table at `$32454` in [the disassembly](DreamsOfPower-Born.asm)). A literal run (`0`, then a count in 2-bit steps, 3 means "more") is always followed by a match; a match is a 2-bit length code, and for length 4 or more a 1-bit choice between a 7-bit and a long offset, plus extra 3-bit length steps. 2. The result is an executable with one **CHIP code hunk of 80,224 bytes** (380 relocations) and a 4-byte BSS hunk. The header allocates them with `AllocMem()` (with `MEMF_CHIP` as the hunk asks), copies the data, applies the relocations, frees the packed data, links the new hunks into the process (`cli_Module`), and jumps to the first one. [decrunch.py](work/decrunch.py) follows the 68000 code step by step; the stream is used up exactly when the output is complete. So, unlike many packers of the time, the outer layer is clean: the problems are in the program itself. ## The program The code hunk starts with code (up to about `$1B2C`, the ProTracker replay included), then the variables, the copper list (`$1C94`), a packed block (`$2334`) and the scrolltext (`$1292C`). ### Memory it takes without asking The first thing the program does is unpack the block at `$2334` (with a **ByteKiller** depacker, the routine at `$2F8`) **to the fixed address `$55000`**: 111,188 bytes of graphics and music, up to `$70254`. It then uses `$70254`–`$7E0B4` as screen memory. In all it takes **168 KB of chip RAM, `$55000`–`$7E0B4`, that it never allocates**, and at the exit it clears it. | Address | Content | Name in the rebuild | |---|---|---| | `$55000` | logo, 256×84, 4 bitplanes | `Data55` | | `$57A00` | palette of the logo (16 colours) | `Pal1` | | `$57A20` | scroller font, 320×160, 3 bitplanes | `FontGfx` | | `$5C520` | palette of the scroller (8 colours) | `Pal3` | | `$5C530` | floppy disks, 320×64, 3 bitplanes | `DiskGfx` | | `$5E330` | palette of the disks (8 colours) | `Pal2` | | `$5E340` | sine table, 1,256 bytes, and a second copy | `SineTab` | | `$5ED10` | skyline, one bitplane | `BarPlane` | | `$5EF48`, `$5F208` | the two bitplanes of the equalizer | `EqPlane1`, `EqPlane2` | | `$5F4CC` | ProTracker module "going strong", 68,968 bytes | `MtModule` | | `$70254` | logo screen, 4 bitplanes | `Screens` | | `$73C14`, `$78054` | the rows of disks (two playfields) | `BgPlanes`, `MidPlanes` | | `$7C494` | scroller screen, 3 bitplanes | `WavePlanes` | If anything else lives there (the program's own hunk, a stack, the buffers of a disk drive or of a filesystem) it is overwritten. With the 512 KB of chip RAM of an A500 there is usually room above the loaded program; on an A600 with three more floppy drives, started from the ItaloDisco menu, the intro freezes with the logo half drawn and no scroller. ### How the intro works - **Start-up**: unpacks the data, `Forbid()`, opens `graphics.library`, saves `gb_LOFlist` (offset 50) and puts its own copper list there, so that the OS loads it every frame. It fades the colours in, draws the rows of disks into their screens once, builds the per-line part of the copper list, initialises the music and puts its level 3 handler at `$6C`. The handler calls `mt_music` and then jumps to the old vector, with a `JMP` whose address is written into the code. - **Main loop**: waits while the beam is outside lines `$80`–`$F0` (`CMPI.B #$F0,VHPOSR` / `BGT`, a signed comparison), then moves the logo halves (`MoveBars`), the scroller (`Scroller`), the wave (`WaveLogo`), the equalizer lines (`EqLines`) and the disks (`Parallax`). In FS-UAE it runs exactly once per frame on an A500 and on an A1200 alike (2,503 loops in 2,502 frames, 2,790 in 2,789, measured with the CIA-A time-of-day counter). - **Logo**: the copper list shows it twice, the top half from line `$21` and the bottom half from line `$4A`, each with its own bitplane pointers and `BPLCON1` scroll, computed from the sine table, so that the two halves swing independently. - **Disks**: a dual-playfield area (6 bitplanes, `BPLCON0` = `$6400`) with two rows that scroll at 1 and 2 pixels per frame, and a third row below at 4 pixels per frame. - **Equalizer**: `mt_music` sets a level for each channel when it plays a note, `EqDecay` lowers it by 5 every frame, and `EqLines` draws four lines with the blitter's line mode (`DrawLine`). - **Scroller and wave**: `Scroller` draws the characters with the blitter into `WavePlanes` (each character is 1 or 2 cells of 16×32 pixels, from `FontTab`); the copper list has 40 lines, each one loading the three bitplane pointers of the scroller with an offset read from the sine table (`WaveLogo`), which bends the text into a wave. Commands in the scrolltext (`|` followed by a letter and a digit): | Command | Effect | |---|---| | `|sN` | speed, N pixels per frame | | `|pN` | length of the wave: step in the sine table, N×10 | | `|aN` | height of the wave, N×2 | | `|wN` | pause the scroller for N×40 frames | | `$00` | start the text again | ### Music "**going strong**": a 31-sample ProTracker module, 68,968 bytes, 12 samples, 18 patterns, 37 positions. The sample names show where the sounds come from: `st-04:440THICK-BK`, `st-06:Snare13`, `st-06:HighHat4`, `st-20:DDM220WoodBlock`, `st-04:Klick`, `st-01:FunBass`, `st-15:strike2`, `st-19:Tidpip`, `st-01:Magic`, `st-01:Gato`, `st-03:cl-mtrumpet`, `st-01:PopBass`. The replay is the standard ProTracker one, with an extra call to `EqDecay` for the equalizer. ### The scrolltext [work/assets/scrolltext.txt](work/assets/scrolltext.txt). It begins with "HI !!! A NEW GROUP IS BORN !!! ANOTHER ???", insists that this one is different "BECAUSE IT'S AN ITALIAN ONE !!", and then spells out the name, slowly and with a big wave: "DREAMS OF POWER". To contact the group you have to write a message, put it in a bottle ("POSSIBLY OF BEER"), and throw it into the sea, then "WAIT AND HOPE" ("REMEMBER YOU MUST CORK IT !!!"). It greets Reflex / Altered Brains for the intro, then Altered Brains, Anonymia, Ghostly Spreaders, Italian Cracking Service, Masterforce, Phaze 101 and Zero Defects, and gives the address to write on the bottle: *Dreams of Power, Via Foro Boario 3, 48022 Lugo, Ravenna, Italy*. ## Assets All in [work/assets/](work/assets): | File | Content | |---|---| | `going_strong.mod` | the music, ready to play in any ProTracker player | | `logo.png` | the DREAMS OF POWER logo, 256×84, 16 colours | | `font.png` | the scroller font, 320×160, 8 colours, enlarged 2× | | `fonttab.txt` | where each character is in the font, and how wide it is | | `disks.png` | the five floppy disks of the parallax, 320×64, 8 colours, enlarged 2× | | `palettes.txt` | the three palettes | | `scrolltext.txt` | the scrolltext, with its commands | ## The relocatable rebuild [work/dreams.asm](work/dreams.asm) is the program as vasm source: - every address is a label; the 168 KB at `$55000`–`$7E0B4` are now two hunks of the program: `data55` (`DATA_C`, 111,188 bytes, the graphics and the music **already unpacked**, from `data_55000.bin`) and `screens` (`BSS_C`, 56,928 bytes); - the code, the variables and the scrolltext are a `CODE` hunk that can go to any memory; the copper list is a small `DATA_C` hunk; - the bitplane pointers in the copper list are constant words in the original: the macro `CPTR` leaves them zero and records them in a table, and `FixCopper` fills them in at start-up; - the per-line part of the copper list (`CopWave`) set only the low words of the three scroller pointers, which works only if the scroller screen does not cross a 64 KB boundary; each line now sets both halves (32 bytes per line instead of 20), and `BuildWaveCop` and `WaveLogo` write both. Since the block at `$55000` is stored already unpacked, the packed copy and the depacker are not needed at run time. ### Memory | | Original | Rebuild | |---|---|---| | allocated | 80,228 bytes chip (code hunk + 4-byte BSS) | 11,792 any + 2,176 chip (copper) + 111,188 chip + 56,928 chip | | taken without allocating | 168,116 bytes chip at `$55000` | – | | total | 248,344 | 182,084 | ### How it was checked Every block that had to change keeps the original instructions in an `IFD ORIGINAL` part. `make verify`: 1. assembles the source with `-DORIGINAL` at `ORG 0` (and the data at `$55000`/`$70254`): the result must be **identical, byte for byte, to the code hunk of the unpacked program**; 2. assembles it again at `$100000`, with the data moved by `$100000` too, and compares the two: every difference must be the high word of an address (457 of them). [checkreloc.py](work/checkreloc.py) also scans the source, outside the `ORIGINAL` parts, for numbers that look like addresses in `$40000`–`$7FFFF` and for copper moves that hold the high half of a pointer. Then the rebuild was run on all the machines in [Testing](#testing). ### Bugs in the original and fixes These are fixed in the rebuild and marked `fix:` in the source. | Bug | Effect | Fix | |---|---|---| | The program unpacks to `$55000` and uses `$55000`–`$7E0B4` without allocating it | depends on what is there: on an A600 with three more floppy drives (from the ItaloDisco menu) the intro freezes, the logo half drawn and no scroller; on an A500 with slow RAM, a Guru right after the exit | the data and the screens are hunks of the program | | Bitplane, copper and blitter DMA are never turned on | on KS 1.3 they are already on (the boot CLI screen is open); on KS 2.0 and later, started from the startup-sequence, the shell window is not open yet and bitplane DMA is off: only the copper colours show, no graphics at all. From the ItaloDisco menu it worked only because the menu had left DMA on | `DMACON` = `$83C0` at start, the old value back on exit | | The level 3 vector is written at `$6C` | on a 68010 or later the vectors are at `VBR`, which is not always 0 | `VBR` is read with `MOVEC` (through `Supervisor()`) when the CPU is a 68010 or later; the vector is written at `VBR+$6C` | | The handler jumps on with a `JMP` whose address is written into the code | on a 68020 or later the instruction cache could hold the old instruction | `CacheClearU()` (exec 37+) after writing it | | `mt_end` writes the vector saved by `mt_install`, which is never called, so `$6C` holds 0 until the main code puts the right vector back a few instructions later | a vertical blank interrupt in between jumps to address 0 | `mt_end` does not touch the vector | | `graphics.library` is closed, then `GfxBase` is used to put the copper list back | harmless in practice (the library stays in memory), but wrong | the copper list is put back first | | The player waits for the audio DMA with 300 `DBF` loops | about 6.5 scan lines on a 7 MHz 68000, much less on a faster CPU | waits for 7 changes of the beam line | | The per-line copper list sets only the low words of the bitplane pointers | only works if the scroller screen stays inside one 64 KB bank | both halves (see above) | | No AGA display setup | on AGA machines `FMODE` and the colour bank registers keep the values the OS left | `FMODE` = `$0000`, `BPLCON3` = `$0C00`, `BPLCON4` = `$0011` (OCS defaults; harmless on OCS/ECS) | Left as in the original: - the main loop synchronisation: once per frame on a 68000 and on a 14 MHz 68020, as measured; a much faster CPU could run it twice in some frames; - the packed block and its ByteKiller depacker are still in the source, for the `ORIGINAL` build, but the rebuild does not use them; - an unused routine at `$1176` that loads a file with `dos.library` (probably used while making the intro), and the unused `mt_install`. ## Tools - [IRA](http://aminet.net/package/dev/asm/ira) 2.11, built from source, for the disassembly, with the config in [work/dreams_unpacked.cnf](work/dreams_unpacked.cnf) - [vasm](http://sun.hasenbraten.de/vasm/) and `exe2adf` for the build - FS-UAE 3.1.66 for the tests, and its debugger for the measurements - Python 3 + Pillow for the depackers, the checks and the asset extraction

# Mario's Game Gallery / FUNdamentals — native Windows preservation collection

Version `v2.0.1` is the current accepted dual-edition release. The obsolete Mac-only `v1.0.0` artifact
remains a withdrawn draft and is not endorsed for redistribution.

This repository contains clean native Win32 compatibility ports of Mario's Game Gallery DOS 1.0
and Mario's FUNdamentals Macintosh 1.1. On boot, one self-contained executable offers either
edition. It embeds both complete source resource collections and needs no original disk image,
original executable, emulator, installer, DOS driver, or loose asset file at runtime.

## Dual-edition release

- A native boot selector launches either the 320×200 DOS 1.0 presentation or the 512×384
  Macintosh 1.1 presentation. `--edition=dos` and `--edition=mac` bypass it for deterministic use.
- The DOS route includes the Interplay and Presage cards, original production-credits page, dim and
  live title stages, voiced Mario sequence, board flip, animated C/G/D/B/Y easel menu, five game
  introductions, source character/name panels, all five games, and original reset/replay panels.
  Its source-specific intro input is retained: every key finishes the current title; clicks finish
  Backgammon, Dominoes, Go Fish, and Yacht, while the original Checkers title ignores clicks.
- All 1,806 DOS resources are preserved from the exact PRD/PRS chain: 187 Pak sheets/3,633 frames,
  574 movies/10,614 commands, 278 SND resources, and 12 XMI tracks. The DOS asset dialect is decoded
  directly; no screenshot reconstruction or replacement voice/music library is used.
- The original 16-bit Borland MZ/FBOV executable is not shipped or executed. Its 2,839 relocations,
  133 segment records, 31 overlays, 505 exact export stubs, and 591 conservative overlay entry
  candidates are independently cataloged and mapped to native subsystems. All 2,900 FBOV fixups
  and all 2,839 MZ relocation targets additionally build a fail-closed resident dependency graph;
  overlay thunks and structurally unreachable compiler/system support remain separate from live
  shell, media, and game caller families.
- Shared games use the recovered native rule/AI/dialogue/outcome controllers with edition-specific
  source art, animation, audio, coordinates, hit targets, and shell behavior. Every behavioral
  regression runs against both asset dialects.

## Macintosh 1.1 fidelity rebuild

- The original BrainStorm and Stepping Stone publisher screens, black/fade timing, title stage,
  voiced Mario introduction, original easel menu, and all five animated game title sequences run
  in their source order. The live menu also restores CODE 12's C/G/D/B/Y selection order and
  corresponding 1111-1115 easel-object animations, red active label, matching pointer arm, and
  held selection pose, with arrow keys, letter shortcuts, and Return. Its randomized Mario host
  now includes the source shoe-tap/5004, bow-tie-spin/5006, and independent blink controllers;
  the remaining randomized branch is the source's proven zero-movie/zero-sound no-op.
- Selected-game intro input remains module-specific like the original: Backgammon and Yacht accept
  any key or mouse-down as completion, Dominoes advances its title controller by one pass on
  mouse-down, and Checkers/Go Fish leave their title playback unchanged. The release gate verifies
  those branches from the five raw CODE resources and through the packaged Win32 window. Yacht's
  later scorecard-board opening ("Good luck" / "I go first") is already gameplay, not that
  skippable title: CODE 18 sends its clicks to locked gameplay controls and vanilla does not skip it.
- Name and Yoshi/Koopa selection occur when the first game needs them; Mario finishes the source
  character-choice speech before its modal choice panel is revealed. The player name and the
  source's four persistent options now survive later launches through per-user Windows settings,
  while the character choice remains session-scoped like the original record format. The temporary
  board shown beneath these first-use prompts rolls back its preview random state before the real
  game starts, preventing the shared QuickDraw sequence from being consumed twice.
- In-game Mario hosts now use the original synchronized `MuV `/`Ply ` mouth timelines and embedded
  voice cues; the original New Game and Play Again resource dialogs are restored. Accepting Play
  Again now resets the board in the existing source-style session, preserving later-round dialogue
  state instead of silently constructing a new game.
- Dynamic game labels, player names, score values, prompts, and the name editor now use the
  original Pak 223–228 bitmap glyphs through the recovered CODE 3/15 character-width and placement
  rules. They no longer substitute a scalable Windows font for the source interface lettering.
- CODE 5's About panel now draws PICT 128 at its exact 447x215 size and uses the disk's exact
  System 7 Times-14, Geneva-9, and Monaco-12 bitmap strikes at the recovered QuickDraw baselines,
  colors, divider position, copyright position, and literal `v. 1.1` label. Its complete raster is
  regression-tested; no generic Windows font remains in the renderer.
- All five native game engines are playable. Their source turn pacing now includes asynchronous
  Mario moves, voiced multi-part dialogue, visible dice/deal/reroll sequences, multiple jumps,
  result announcements, source idle prompts and knock-knock conversations, and the original
  end-of-game flow. The recovered control-flow, RNG, dialogue, strategy, replay, and result branches
  are covered by deterministic executable regressions rather than represented as
  instruction-by-instruction translations.
  - Yacht uses the recovered original scoring values (25-point Little Straight, 30-point Big
    Straight, and dice-sum Full House/Four of a Kind) plus CODE 18's exact adviser category order,
    straight/pair retention, duplicate handling, and final-line sacrifice rules. Its ending now uses
    the recovered tie/player/Mario result pools, the player-only movie-6022 celebration with timed
    effects, the shared replay question, and the source's progressive scorecard wipe. Its complete
    source dialogue RNG is also restored: Good Luck/I Go First opening, optional first-turn line,
    shuffled thinking and score-reaction pools, conditional reroll speech, 80-tick idle prompts,
    and the original Pizza/Jamaica/Giovanni/Yucca knock-knock cycle.
    Its dice controller uses the original white-reroll/red-held lanes, sequential Mario selection
    effects, remaining-roll markers, pre-roll hand gesture, player-owned twelve-round lifecycle,
    delayed Mario score commits, and progressive five-die player-win reveal. Eight deterministic
    full matches per edition exercise those controls through real roll, die, and scorecard clicks
    and require both twelve-line scorecards plus the result controller to complete.
- Go Fish now follows CODE 17's recovered greeting/"I'm-a go first" opening, shuffled dialogue
  pools, its four-cards-per-rank numbering with source Pak 5006 corner numerals, 300-pair source
  deck swap, contiguous source deal,
  persistent thirteen-record hand layout (including the rotated seven-card opening order, fixed
  54x76 hit targets, overflow row, duplicate consolidation, gap preservation, and first-free-record
  reuse),
  rank-suffix tables and 1-in-4 `Do you have any...` branch, remembered player questions,
  nonrepeating Mario request history (including the source's discarded `Random(0)` seed advance),
  forced-refill paths, requested-card extra turns, and deck-empty book-count outcome rule. Its
  120-tick idle controller alternates the two impatient lines with the original 5094/5091/5090
  visual pool and its two intentional no-op entries, retaining selector state across replay. Its
  player-win ending now deals the source Pak 5211
  “YOU WIN!” card faces, flips them away together with seven synchronized copies of movie 5210,
  and asks for another game; Mario-win and tie branches retain their intentionally shorter endings.
- Backgammon opens with CODE 11's two warm-up passes, lazy `[3,4,0]` greeting selector (movies
  11603/11604/11600), and fixed movie 11618, “Let's roll to see who goes first.” It then paints its
  eight starting stacks in exact source-record order, starting sound 5042 once per stack and
  exposing one checker on every following controller pass. The board keeps all fifteen possible
  checker actors per point and uses CODE 11's decoded 24-point egg/shell bases, point-dependent
  lean, and two-pixel offsets between groups of five for both drawing and movement, instead of
  collapsing larger stacks into a numeric counter. Ordinary non-double Mario rolls use
  `$1320`'s recovered `[32,31,30]` thinking pool; the `[5,7,9]` praise branch belongs to unreachable
  `$121C` and is not substituted into live play. The game then uses CODE 11's recovered ordered move
  selector—bar-entry hits, point making, blot
  consolidation, safe moves, contact play, and source-order bearing off—instead of a substitute
  numerical board evaluator. As in the original controller, the selector is re-entered after every
  individual die rather than prefiltering turns through modern maximum-move rules. Its complete
  game-over controller is also restored: source outcome lines, the simultaneous 4022/4023
  player-victory movies and timed effect, branch-specific pauses, Mario's replay question, and only
  then the original Play Again dialog. Its idle controller now alternates by source draw between
  the three nonrepeating full-body Mario movies and three nonrepeating voiced prompts; the invented
  Backgammon knock-knock path has been removed. The two-click input controller resolves a selected
  checker's legal destination before treating an occupied point as another selection, so building
  onto friendly stacks works as in CODE 11. Eight full matches per edition exercise the public roll,
  point, bar, and bearing-off controls through the native result sequence.
- Dominoes uses CODE 14's exact three-pass 84-call tile swap, dealt-half doublet guarantee,
  backward alternating deal, deal/opening speech draws, hand-order candidate enumeration, and
  smallest-exposed-pip selection, including the original random side choice when a tile fits both
  chain ends. Player placement restores the original drag controller, including its dynamic
  endpoint radius, right-side distance ties, and pip-based choice when a wrapped chain's ends
  overlap. Its recovered turn controller restores probabilistic Mario/player handoffs, the
  one-time thinking line and delay, repeated-draw RNG consumption, four-way pass comments,
  first/later player-draw behavior, move-comment repeat suppression, and the exact timed idle
  prompts/four-joke cycle. Its complete last-tile and blocked-game result controller uses the
  source's weighted speech pools, score/tie branches, delays, and two replay questions. Either
  kind of player win follows CODE 14's common effect-5023 gate, SONG/XMI 135 switch, authored
  movie-3900 result actor, and three-pass hold before replay; all other branches retain gameplay
  music. Drawn
  bones remain visible and draggable through all fourteen Macintosh or sixteen DOS hand records;
  at capacity minus one, the source `$5744`/DOS `$5367` boneyard swap guarantees that the final
  permitted draw is playable instead of leaving a full-hand softlock. A 128-seed live match sweep
  per edition drives the actual draw and drag/drop routes while enforcing the complete 28-tile
  inventory and chain adjacency after every controller pass.
- Checkers uses CODE 16's recovered full-path move generator and depth-limited minimax scoring,
  including mandatory multi-jumps, optional partial jumps when Forced Jumps is disabled,
  king/crowning weights, source board-scan order, and its 50% equal-score replacement rule. Its
  ending now distinguishes eliminating Mario from leaving him
  unable to move, uses the ten-line player-win and first/later Mario-win pools, clears the board in
  source order after an elimination, and reaches the original two-line replay pool before the
  Play Again dialog. Its source-timed idle controller restores the three full-body animations, two
  impatient lines, ordered four-joke cycle, inter-line pauses, and exact random follow-up delays.
  The former invented 80-quiet-move draw shortcut has been removed.
- Play Again resets each board/deck/score controller in place. Dual-edition regressions cover every
  game and preserve only its source-owned session state: later-round counters, lazy dialogue pools,
  idle cycles, player identity, and options.
- Original game backgrounds, characters, cards, dice, pieces, scorecards, voices, effects, and music
  are decoded from the supplied image rather than replaced with lookalike art.
- The original QuickDraw pseudorandom generator, CODE 1 range scaler, CODE 13 startup stirring and
  descending shuffle, plus game-local swap routines drive dice rolls, deals, AI ties, and dialogue
  selectors; deterministic source vectors are checked by the release self-test.
- All 1,707 original Macintosh resources embedded in one deterministic archive.
- Runtime decoders for all 180 proprietary `Pak ` resources (3,166 frames).
- Runtime support for 467 `MuV `/`Ply `/`Img ` movies (8,586 commands), including layered images, offsets, timing, and sound events.
- Runtime conversion/playback for all 313 classic Mac `snd ` resources, including concurrent voices;
  all 666 movie sound events and direct startup/gameplay routes are audited. A fail-closed source
  scan pins all 65 absolute calls as 45 tracked `$A18` replacements and 20 `$CAA` direct effects.
  CODE 1's `$B22` direct-channel busy gate prevents the 105 ms menu-selection click from
  overlapping itself on 33 ms pointer steps.
- In-memory WinMM sequencing for all 11 standard MIDI resources with the recovered non-sequential
  `SONG` routing for menu, gameplay, and player-win tracks—no temporary files. The Windows MIDI
  mapper is prewarmed asynchronously, so a slow software-synth initialization cannot freeze the
  startup transition between the publisher card and Mario's title sequence. Every Macintosh and
  DOS outcome branch is regression-tested for its exact primary/win route, and Play Again must
  restore the selected game's primary track.
- Original title, credits, icon, startup, menu, title-sequence, and gameplay art in the native UI.
- All nine source-authored help pages and the game-specific File/Edit/Options menu functions are
  restored, together with the PICT 128 About and PICT 129 Credits presentations and their original
  jingles, including name-field clipboard editing, Change Name, independent Sound/Music,
  Hide Background, Animated Pieces, and Checkers Forced Jumps.
- The recovered CODE 7 `mPRF` behavior is ported without a required sidecar file: Sound, Music,
  Hide Background, Animated Pieces, and the source editor's 15-character player name are persisted
  under the current Windows user. Hidden QA runs deliberately do not read or overwrite those values
  and forcibly mute voices, effects, and MIDI.
- DPI-scaled output uses a deterministic nearest-neighbour presentation buffer, preventing the
  one-pixel frame-to-frame shimmer produced by fractional GDI stretching. A persistent full-client
  back buffer is committed in one blit, so Windows repaints cannot expose the black clear or a
  partially rendered frame.
- No translated 68k code is executed by the port.

The executable is a self-contained native fidelity target for both supplied editions. It
semantically replaces the original 68k/8086 code and Macintosh/DOS platform services; it does not
embed or run either original application executable. See
[the function audit](docs/FUNCTION_AUDIT.md) for the evidence and coverage statement.

The supplied `MarioFundamentals.img` is the exact emulator-start image from the linked Internet
Archive item: its 25,165,824-byte size, MD5 `EEAD810A2DF2FD4B6ED62D52F363F74C`, and SHA-1
`4423EDDDE3BE15D80EF2822B2DB861BF094FB2F4` all match the Archive.org metadata. Its independently
recorded SHA-256 is `2F898FEC2605D9855D67DF69F6E90BD4D97BFF7E5199163A3462BC2DBA64F0A7`.

The DOS source set is pinned independently: the supplied fixed VHD is 8,389,120 bytes with SHA-256
`092C319B1EE2FBA79F12648AE1757953A6C7A2A837B5E38C7418169FC434085A`; its CD CHD is
221,698,560 bytes with SHA-256
`A31033A28F3B1BC4744D36B90FD4B6867EBC236E8A7F754235E6D1A5881EB466`. The matching game core is
MARIO.EXE/PRD/PRS with hashes recorded in
[the reverse-engineering report](docs/REVERSE_ENGINEERING.md).

## Build and run

Requirements:

- Windows 10 or later
- CMake 3.24+
- Ninja
- A MinGW-w64 C++20 compiler

From PowerShell:

```powershell
.\tools\build_release.ps1
.\dist\MarioFundamentals.exe
```

The gate defaults to Ninja. On an equivalent MinGW environment it can use the installed make
generator without changing any checks: `-CMakeGenerator "MinGW Makefiles"`.

The release script configures a static C++ runtime build, compiles the resources, runs the
executable's full hidden/silent self-test, verifies the PE architecture and dependency set, proves
both deterministic asset packs occur exactly once, proves all 1,707 Macintosh and 1,806 DOS ripped
resources against their extraction manifests when those local audit records are present, reruns the
self-test from an empty working directory, decodes and verifies all 3,149 Macintosh loader
relocations and regenerates the 936-row global function ledger when raw CODE/DATA evidence is
present, regenerates 246 Macintosh and 237 DOS no-window
presentation frames at the exact 512×384 and 320×200 logical sizes, verifies the filename/length/
content digest of every one of those 483 deterministic frames, inventories all 225 retained
vanilla captures, compares 53 independent original-output cases (publisher/title states and the
terminal open-hand cel, pressed-menu feedback, exact pointer traversal/retargeting and selection
holds, stable layouts, source-timed game intros, first-use panels,
Backgammon setup, Go Fish scoreboard captions/questions/transfers, exact Dominoes portrait
registration, and focused Macintosh Yacht actor/hand/dice/marker/gesture/pre-roll/cup checks) when those
unshipped local captures are present, and copies the result to `dist`.

Every push to `main` and every pull request also runs this dual-edition release gate on a clean
GitHub-hosted Windows runner. The workflow is validation-only: it uploads no executable, creates no
release, and cannot create or modify a GitHub release. Source-media preservation, disassembly, and
independent-reference checks remain additional local requirements because their evidence is
deliberately excluded from the repository.

The accepted dual-edition release artifact is written to `dist`, with its build-specific checksum
in `dist/SHA256SUMS.txt`. Any rebuilt candidate requires the same corrected-presentation audit and
explicit acceptance before it replaces the published artifact. The hidden self-test runs from an
otherwise empty directory containing only the executable, proving that no disk image, original
application, DOS support file, loose asset, or generated sidecar is required at runtime.

For that required human review, generate the checksum-bound, lossless contact-sheet packet after
the gate passes:

```powershell
python .\tools\build_visual_acceptance_packet.py
```

Then open `work/qa/visual-acceptance/index.html` and follow the live-play checklist in
[the visual acceptance procedure](docs/VISUAL_ACCEPTANCE.md). Passing the automated gate alone does
not authorize publishing a replacement build.

To run only the executable-level audit:

```powershell
Start-Process .\build\MarioFundamentals.exe -ArgumentList '--self-test' -WindowStyle Hidden -Wait
```

To regenerate the silent logical-resolution presentation sweeps without creating a window or
opening an audio device:

```powershell
Start-Process .\build\MarioFundamentals.exe -ArgumentList '--render-mac-qa' -WindowStyle Hidden -Wait
Start-Process .\build\MarioFundamentals.exe -ArgumentList '--render-dos-qa' -WindowStyle Hidden -Wait
```

The expected report begins:

```text
PASS mac_assets=1707 mac_pak=180 mac_frames=3166 mac_movies=467 mac_commands=8586 mac_midi_events=6968 mac_sounds=313 games=5 dos_assets=1806 dos_pak=187 dos_frames=3633 dos_movies=574 dos_commands=10614 dos_xmi_events=12253 dos_sounds=278
```

## Controls

- Boot selector: choose Macintosh 1.1 or DOS 1.0; closing it exits without starting either game.
- Mouse: select games, pieces, cards, dice, score lines, and buttons.
- Main menu: arrow keys cycle in source C/G/D/B/Y order; those letters select directly; `Enter`
  starts the selected game.
- `S`: toggle sound and voices.
- `M`: toggle music independently.
- `H`: hide/show the backing presentation by switching to the original-size compact game window.
- `F1`: show rules for the current game.

## 1. Start und Hauptschleife

### 1.1 Startup (Segment 1000)
`entry @ 1000:0000` ist der normale Turbo-C-Startcode (c0l): DOS-Version (INT 21h/30h), Speicher
schrumpfen (4Ah), BSS nullen, Interruptvektoren 0/4/5/6 sichern (`FUN_1000_012f`), `_setupio`/Init-Tabellen
über Funktionszeiger `[0x1944]`/`[0x1948]`, Timer-Tick lesen (INT 1Ah), dann

```

FUN_4519_0010()                   ; == exit()
```

Weitere Funktionen in Seg 1000 sind Turbo-C-Runtime-Helfer:

| Adresse | Vorschlag | Bemerkung |
|---|---|---|
| 1000:0412 | `LXMUL@` | 32-bit Multiplikation (sehr häufig) |
| 1000:042b / 042f / 0434 / 0439 | `LDIV@` / `LUDIV@` / `LMOD@` / `LUMOD@` | 32-bit Division |
| 1000:0396 | `PADA@` (huge pointer add) | nur aus der Heap-Lib (4520/4551/4589) |
| 1000:03f1 | `PCMP@`/Normalisierung | nur Heap-Lib |
| 1000:04ce / 050a | `LXLSH@` / `LXRSH@` | 32-bit Shifts |
| 1000:0529 | `SCOPY@` | Struct-Kopie (`rep movsw`) |

Ablauf:
1. `atexit`-ähnliche Registrierung (`FUN_451d_0003` = `atexit_far`) von Cleanup-Routinen:

---

## 4. Globale Datenstrukturen (DGROUP)

Alle Strukturen sind als flache Arrays mit manuellem Stride codiert (Turbo C hat die Struct-Zugriffe
zu `basis + i*stride + feld` aufgelöst). Index 0 ist meist unbenutzt (Spieler 1..3).

| Adresse | Stride × Anzahl | Bedeutung |
|---|---|---|
| `0x8bbc` | 23 B × 4 | Spieler-Stammdaten; `+0x14` = ausgeschieden-Flag (0 = aktiv) |
| `0x7b22` | 30 B (0xf Worte) × 3+ | Figur im Hochhaus: `+2` Etage, `+4` x, `+6` Ziel, `+0xc` Zustand, `+0x10` Raum/Tür, `+0x12` Richtung … |
| `0x71d5` | 4 B (long) × 4 | **Kontostand** je Spieler (`money_add`) |
| `0x43f7` | 0x5a B × 4 | **Sendeplan** heute: 15 Worte Programm-ID je Stunde (`<1000` Film, `≥1000` Serie+1000), danach Status-/Werbe-Arrays (`+0x1e`) |
| `0x3919` | 0x5a B × 4 | zweiter Plan (morgen/gestern (?)) |
| `0x6ef9` | 0x6c B × 4 | **Archiv** je Spieler nach Genre (10 Genres × 4 Plätze), Zähler `0x6f59` |
| `0x1b50` | 0x46 B × 4 | Liste à 7-Byte-Einträge (Zähler `0x7688`) – Werbeverträge (?) |
| `0x65af` | 0x5a B × 15 | Tabelle mit ID-Suche (`2bd1_30b8/314c`) – Werbung/Verträge (?) |
| `0x63c5` | 10 B × 49 | Tabelle mit ID-Suche (`2bd1_3024`) (?) |
| `0x609f` | 26 B × n | Nachrichten an den Spieler (Typ-ID, bis 10 Parameter, Tag, Stunde) |
| `0x74ca`, `0x7690`, `0x6d89` | 0x20 B × 4 | Zuschauerstatistik pro Stunde / Tag, 7-Tage-Historie |
| `0x248d` | 10 B × 4 | Quote der laufenden Stunde je Spieler |
| `0x1ce0`, `0x1ce9` | 0x1ce B × 4 | Zuschauerpotential je Stunde / Werbeslots (?) |
| `0x2463` / `0x732a` | Wort-Liste | Angebot beim Filmhändler |
| `0x7468` | 4 Worte | Wettbewerb (alle 3 Tage, `2bd1_408e`) |
| `0x24c5[p]`, `0x24e7` | Byte | KI-Zustand je Spieler, aktuell bearbeiteter KI-Spieler |
| `0x71c4` | int | Spieltag; `0x71ca`/`0x71cc` Stunde/Minute |
| `0x7bd6/7bd8` | int | Mausposition; `0x7af4` Klick |
| `0x8e62…0x8ec0` | far ptr | Offscreen-Bitmaps (Status, Cursor-Hintergrund, Dialoge) |

Filmdatensatz (23 Byte, far-Array `DAT_2489`): `+0` Genre (char), `+1` Qualität/Preisfaktor, `+3` Jahr/Faktor,
`+5` Zustand, `+6/+7` **Bitfelder** (u. a. Bit 5 „im Besitz/verwendet“, Bit 7, Bits in `+7`), `+8` long Preis,
`+0xe`, `+0xf`, `+0x11`. Seriendatensatz (57 Byte, `DAT_2626`): Titel ab `+0`, `+0x24` Zustand, `+0x25/+0x26` Bitfelder,
`+0x27` long, `+0x31` aktuelle Folge.

---

## 5. Portierungsrisiken / Auffälligkeiten

1. **Ghidra-Switch-Tabellen kaputt (größtes Analyseproblem).** Turbo C erzeugt `jmp cs:[bx+tab]` mit der
   Tabelle direkt im Code (28 Stellen: 1054×3, 1581×4, 1f51×6, 239a×2, 27bb×4, 2bd1×3, 340d×1, 3b0a×3, 3f95×2)
   sowie 6 „sparse switches“ (`mov cx,n; mov bx,tab; cmp ax,cs:[bx]; loop`, Werte- + Zieltabelle, z. B. 1581:00cd).
   Ghidra dekodiert die Tabellen als Code → Pseudo-`swi()`, `in()/out()`, „overlapping instructions“,
   Funktionen mit 4 000–29 000 Zeilen (`1054_0e4c`, `1f51_1703`, `3f95_174b`, `3f95_19f7`, `3b0a_3854`, …)
   und fehlende Funktionen (`1581_2220`, `1581_23ca`, `19e6_1be9`). Die `swi/in/out`-Treffer in 1054/1581/1f51/
   2bd1/340d/3f95 sind **Artefakte**, keine echten Hardwarezugriffe. → Vor der Detailanalyse ein Ghidra-Skript,
   das die Tabellen als Daten markiert und die Sprungziele als Referenzen setzt, danach neu dekompilieren.
2. **Registerparameter**: Die HES-I/O-Lib (44ce/4500/4505/450b/4510) bekommt die Dateinummer in AX; Ghidra
   zeigt `void`-Signaturen. Die Aufrufer übergeben die Werte aber korrekt auf dem Stack (Turbo-C-Wrapper).
3. **Direkter Videozugriff nur in den Bibliotheken**: Mode 13h (320×200×256), Segment 0xA000 (`43d5_0008`),
   Blits in 8-Pixel-Einheiten (`x>>3`), Palette über INT 10h/1012h, Retrace-Warten über Port 0x3DA (`43d2`).
   Die Spielmodule arbeiten ausschließlich über `1f51`-Wrapper → gut durch SDL-Surface ersetzbar.
4. **Software-Mauszeiger** (Hintergrund sichern/restaurieren in `game_tick`), Maus via INT 33h, Tastatur via INT 16h.
5. **Timer-ISR** (Lib 42fe/43ae) zählt `DAT_9014`; die gesamte Spielzeit hängt daran (`50/speed`-Ticks).
   Portierung: durch `SDL_GetTicks()`-basierten Zähler (18,2 Hz oder der programmierte PIT-Takt – noch prüfen) ersetzen.
6. **Viele modale Warteschleifen**, die selbst `game_tick()` aufrufen (z. B. Diskettenwechsel `1c74_0457`,
   Dialoge, Fahrstuhl) → für SDL muss die Event-Pumpe in `game_tick`/`input_poll` sitzen; ein Umbau auf
   eine echte Hauptschleife ist nicht nötig, wenn man diese Struktur beibehält.
7. **Far-Pointer überall** (large model): Datenbanken (`DAT_2489`, `DAT_2626`, `DAT_713c`) und alle Bitmaps sind
   far; Ghidra zeigt `CONCAT22(seg,off)`/`_2_2_`-Zerlegung. Huge-Pointer-Arithmetik (`PADA@`) nur im Heap.
   Port: einfache Zeiger, `farcalloc/farfree` → `calloc/free`.
8. **Bitfelder und gepackte Structs** (Film-/Serien-Records mit 23/57 Byte, Bitfelder in Wort `+6/+7`, die sich
   überlappen) – im Port `#pragma pack(1)` bzw. explizites (De-)Serialisieren; Savegame-Format (`3077_11d2`)
   packt die Bitfelder zusätzlich um.
9. **16-Bit-Arithmetik**: `int` = 16 Bit, Geld als 32-Bit-`long` (LXMUL/LDIV). Überläufe/Vorzeichen
   (z. B. `hour_index`, Preise) beim Port mit `int16_t`/`int32_t` exakt nachbilden.
10. **Globals mit festen DGROUP-Offsets** und Arrays mit Index 0 unbenutzt; Ghidra meldet „Globals overlap
    smaller symbols“ – mehrere Strukturen werden über dieselben Adressen mit unterschiedlicher Breite gelesen.
11. **Kein selbstmodifizierender Code** gefunden (lineare Capstone-Durchsicht aller Spielsegmente: keine Stores
    nach `cs:`, keine echten `in/out/int`; die einzigen Treffer sind dekodierte Sprungtabellen). Einziger
    CS-Store ist der Turbo-C-Standard `DGROUP@` im Startup (1000:0003). Kein Inline-Assembler in den Spielmodulen erkennbar; Assembler steckt nur in den Libs.
12. **Sprach-/Diskettenlogik**: Dateinummer < 301 → Diskette 1, sonst Diskette 2 (Dialog); im Port entfernen.
13. Debug-Rest: unbekannter `#`-Specifier im Formatter erzeugt den String „Fuck“ (DS:0d1a).

---

## 6. Empfohlene nächste Schritte
1. Ghidra-Skript `FixSwitchTables.java`: alle `2E FF A7 xx xx` und `2E 3B 07`-Muster suchen, Tabellenlänge aus
   dem vorangehenden `cmp ax,imm` bzw. `mov cx,imm` lesen, Tabelle als `word[]` definieren, Ziele als
   Code/Funktion anlegen, Jump-References setzen → erneut exportieren.
2. Türtabelle (`DS:0x7c80/0x7ca8`) dekodieren und Raum-IDs mit den Raumnamen aus HES 253 verknüpfen.
3. Structs in Ghidra anlegen: `Film` (23 B), `Series` (57 B), `Figure` (30 B), `PlayerInfo` (23 B), `Schedule` (0x5a B).
4. Formatter `1d41_0003` vollständig dokumentieren (Specifier-Tabelle bei DS:0153, Handler-Tabelle +12).

# UC2 DOS → Linux Port — NOTES

UltraCompressor II (UC2) was a 1994 Borland C++ / DOS application. This
directory contains a **port to Linux (g++)**. The Borland / real-mode run-time
has been replaced, the performance-critical 80386 assembly routines have been
rewritten in C, and the compression/decompression engine works end-to-end
(create, list, test, extract — verified by round-trip).

## Build
```
make            # builds ./uc2 (ncurses required: -lncurses)
```
The build produces `./uc2`; `make test` (from the repository root) runs a
round-trip smoke test.

## Multi-volume (SAS) format

`src/uc2sas.cpp` reproduces the piece format of the original **SAS.EXE**
("simple archive splitter") shipped with **UC PRO v2.3** (`uc2pro.exe`, free for
individual use): <http://www.bttr-software.de/freesoft/arc1.htm>. The 14-byte
piece header was reverse-engineered from that binary for interoperability;
`uc2 split` / `uc2 join` are byte-interchangeable with SAS.EXE in both
directions.

# DIFF_FROM_ORIGINAL

Accepted, intentional deviations of the TypeScript port from the original DOS game.
The behavioral oracle is the public-domain Delphi reconstruction (`Pole2/PoleWin32.dpr`);
where that reconstruction itself deviated from DOS (per `Pole2/Readme.md`), the port
follows DOS unless noted. Full policy with rationale: `docs/architecture.md`.

## Web-platform substitutions (no DOS equivalent possible)

1. **Esc** restarts to the splash screen instead of exiting to DOS (`ExitProcess`).
   As in the original, nothing is persisted on exit.
2. **Tab** (boss key) mutes the sound but cannot minimize the browser window.
3. **Alt+Enter** toggles fullscreen via the browser Fullscreen API instead of the
   Win32/DOS mode switch.
4. **Top-8 list (POLE.PIC)** is updated in session memory only — never written to disk
   (CLAUDE.md hard constraint). Insertion semantics (strict-less, 0-based rank labels,
   `$` suffix, inserted-row highlight) match the original exactly.
5. The two hand-cursor busy-loops yield to the event loop every 10 ms (the original
   busy-waited the CPU); timing of all visible behavior is unaffected.
6. Sound is produced by an 8 kHz PWM synth through WebAudio at a fixed master gain.
   Envelopes, frequencies, durations, and pacing replicate the original routines;
   the speaker timbre is an approximation (parity case `ts-audio-approximation`).

## Evidence-based corrections to the reconstruction

7. **OVL pairing**: words are odd records, themes even records (verified directly
   against POLE.OVL). The literal reconstruction indexing pairs word w+1 with theme w
   and reads out of bounds at the last word; the port uses the verified pairing.

## DOS-first policy calls (reconstruction deviated; port follows DOS, capture-unverified)

8. **Box (шкатулки) trigger**: after 3 successful moves (DOS) rather than 3 opened
   letters (reconstruction), and offered to human seats only.
9. **NPC on СЕКТОР ПРИЗ**: always answers «Играем!» — NPCs never take the prize.
10. **Prize bargaining**: Yakubovich always escalates to МИЛЛИОН before handing over
    the prize (the reconstruction could stop earlier at random).
11. **Player speech**: only NPC seats get speech bubbles; the human plays silently.

## Reconstruction behaviors kept although DOS differed

12. **Player modes.** The web default is «1 игрок + 2 НПС»: only seat 2 is
    prompted for a name and an empty name keeps the seat human as «ИГРОК».
    The settings tab offers «2 игрока (как в оригинале)», which restores the
    original prompts for seats 2–3 with the reconstruction's empty-name → NPC
    fallback (DOS itself kept unnamed seats human). Seat 1 is never prompted
    in any mode, exactly as in the code.
13. **Word-repeat avoidance across stages** (DOS could repeat words): kept; if the
    session question pool has fewer than 8 entries, repeats are allowed to avoid the
    original's selection soft-lock.
14. **Word/round-title centering** and the **board-typed word entry** follow the
    reconstruction; the DOS placement/mechanism is unknown pending captures
    (parity case `ts-text-centering-provisional`).

## Minor

15. The brick-wall pattern was effectively fixed in the original (drawn before the
    RNG was seeded); the port draws it from the seeded RNG stream, so it varies per
    run and follows `?seed=`.
16. The admin question editor sanitizes words to А–Я (a word containing any other
    byte could never be completed or solved by the engine).
17. Sound defaults to OFF — this matches DOS (the reconstruction turned it on by
    default); listed here for visibility, not a deviation.
18. **Wheel spin animation** (dpr:1229-1244): the original travels
    `(random(10)+5) shl 1` = 10..28 half-steps — always under one revolution and
    always an even count, so against the symmetric two-color 16-wedge art every
    spin *looked* like the same two-segment nudge (landing sectors were random;
    the perceived rotation was not). The port prepends two full extra revolutions
    (+64 half-steps ≡ 0 mod 32) at constant speed before the original
    deceleration: the same single `random(10)` draw, the same landing sector,
    and the same RNG stream — only the visible animation is longer. Landings
    stay even-aligned: an odd rest would park the arrow exactly between two
    sector icons (verified by rendering).
